For example: dvecattālīsā, dvecattālīsa, dvecattālīsaṃ; and similarly dvācattālīsa, etc. Also dvecattārīsā, dvecattārīsa, dvecattārīsaṃ; and similarly dvācattārīsā, dvācattārīsa, etc. The forms cattālīsati, ekacattālīsati, dvecattālīsati, dvācattālīsati, and so on, are like ekūnavīsati.

3,98. Cattālīsādo vā

3.98. Optionally from forty onwards.

Asatādo nāññatthe cattālīsādo tisse hoti vā. Tecattālīsā tecattālīsa tecattālīsaṃ. Bho tecattālīse iccādi hoti. Evaṃ ticattālīsā tecattārīsā ticattārīsā iccādi, tecattālīsati ticattālīsati iccādi pubbeva.

From forty onwards, and not elsewhere, for ti, e is optionally substituted. For example: tecattālīsā, tecattālīsa, tecattālīsaṃ. The form bho tecattālīse, etc., also occurs. Similarly, ticattālīsā, tecattārīsā, ticattārīsā, etc., and tecattālīsati, ticattālīsati, etc., as before.

Evaṃ catucattālīsā pañcacattālīsā catucattālīsati pañcacattālīsati iccādi yāva ekūnapaññāsā.

Thus: catucattālīsā (forty-four) and pañcacattālīsā (forty-five); catucattālīsati and pañcacattālīsati, and so on, up to ekūnapaññāsā (forty-nine).

Paññāsā [M 0.0096] paññāsa paññāsaṃ iccādi hoti. Evaṃ dvepaññāsā dvāpaññāsā dvipaññāsā dvepaṇṇāsā dvāpaṇṇāsā dvipaṇṇāsā. Tepaññāsā tipaññāsā tipaññāsaṃ tepaṇṇāsā tipaṇṇāsā. Catupaṇṇāsā pañcapaṇṇāsā iccādi yāva ekūnasaṭṭhi.

The forms paññāsā, paññāsa, paññāsaṃ, etc., occur (for fifty). Similarly, for fifty-two: dvepaññāsā, dvāpaññāsā, dvipaññāsā, dvepaṇṇāsā, dvāpaṇṇāsā, dvipaṇṇāsā. For fifty-three: tepaññāsā, tipaññāsā, tipaññāsaṃ, tepaṇṇāsā, tipaṇṇāsā. Catupaṇṇāsā (fifty-four), pañcapaṇṇāsā (fifty-five), and so on, up to ekūnasaṭṭhi (fifty-nine).

Evaṃ saṭṭhi, ekasaṭṭhi, dvesaṭṭhi dvāsaṭṭhi dvisaṭṭhi, tesaṭṭhi tisaṭṭhi, catusaṭṭhi pañcasaṭṭhi iccādi yāva ekūnasattati.

Similarly, saṭṭhi (sixty), ekasaṭṭhi (sixty-one); for sixty-two: dvesaṭṭhi, dvāsaṭṭhi, dvisaṭṭhi; for sixty-three: tesaṭṭhi, tisaṭṭhi; catusaṭṭhi (sixty-four), pañcasaṭṭhi (sixty-five), and so on, up to ekūnasattati (sixty-nine).

Sattati, ekasattati, dvesattati dvāsattati dvisattati, tesattati tisattati. Dvesattari dvāsattari dvisattari, catusattati, pañcasattati, catusattari, pañcasattarīti yāva ekūnāsīti.

Sattati (seventy), ekasattati (seventy-one); for seventy-two: dvesattati, dvāsattati, dvisattati; for seventy-three: tesattati, tisattati. Also, for seventy-two: dvesattari, dvāsattari, dvisattari; catusattati (seventy-four), pañcasattati (seventy-five), catusattari (seventy-four), pañcasattari (seventy-five), and so on, up to ekūnāsīti (seventy-nine).

Asīti, ekāsīti, dvāsīti, yāgame dviyāsīti, teasīti tiyāsīti, caturāsīti, pañcāsīti iccādi yāva ekūnanavuti.

Asīti (eighty), ekāsīti (eighty-one), dvāsīti (eighty-two), and with the augment y, dviyāsīti; for eighty-three: teasīti, tiyāsīti; caturāsīti (eighty-four), pañcāsīti (eighty-five), and so on, up to ekūnanavuti (eighty-nine).

Navuti, ekanavuti, dvenavuti dvānavuti dvinavuti, tenavuti tinavuti, catunavuti, pañcanavuti iccādi yāva ekūnasataṃ, etaṃ napuṃsakaliṅga+mekavacanantaṃ.

Navuti (ninety), ekanavuti (ninety-one); for ninety-two: dvenavuti, dvānavuti, dvinavuti; for ninety-three: tenavuti, tinavuti; catunavuti (ninety-four), pañcanavuti (ninety-five), and so on, up to ekūnasataṃ (ninety-nine). This last number is of neuter gender and singular.

Sataṃ, bho sata satā, sataṃ, sataṃ. Satena, karaṇe satena. Satassa, satā satamhā satasmā, satassa, sate satamhi satasmiṃ. Evaṃ ekasatato pabhuti yāva sahassaṃ.

Declension of sataṃ (hundred): sataṃ (nominative, accusative); bho sata, satā (vocative); satena (instrumental); satā, satamhā, satasmā (ablative); satassa (genitive); sate, satamhi, satasmiṃ (locative). Thus from one hundred onwards, up to a thousand.

Koṭi pakoṭi koṭippakoṭi akkhobhiṇiyo itthiliṅge+kavacanantā. Vaggabhede tu sabbāsampi saṃkhyānaṃ bahuvacanopi hoteva “dvevīsatiyo jinadantā” “tisso vīsatiyo dinaghaṭikā” iccādi.

Koṭi, pakoṭi, koṭippakoṭi, and akkhobhiṇī are feminine gender and singular. However, when distinguishing groups, all numerals can also be in the plural, as in dvevīsatiyo jinadantā (twenty-two teeth of the Jina) and tisso vīsatiyo dinaghaṭikā (three twenties of day-hours), etc.

Dasadasakaṃ sataṃ nāma, dasasataṃ sahassaṃ nāma, dasasahassaṃ nahutaṃ, dasanahutaṃ lakkhaṃ, satasahassantipi vuccati.

Ten tens are called a sataṃ (hundred); ten hundreds are called a sahassaṃ (thousand); ten thousands are called a nahutaṃ; ten nahutas are called a lakkhaṃ, which is also called a hundred thousand.

Lakkhasataṃ [M 0.0097] koṭi, koṭilakkhasataṃ pakoṭi, pakoṭilakkhasataṃ koṭippakoṭi, evaṃ nahutaṃ, ninnahutaṃ, akkhobhiṇī, bindu, abbudaṃ, nirabbudaṃ, ahahaṃ, ababaṃ, aṭaṭaṃ, sogaṇḍikaṃ, uppalaṃ, kumudaṃ, puṇḍarīkaṃ, padumaṃ, kathānaṃ, mahākathānaṃ, asaṅkhyeyyanti yathākkamaṃ satalakkhaguṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

A hundred lakhs are a koṭi; a hundred lakhs of koṭi are a pakoṭi; a hundred lakhs of pakoṭi are a koṭippakoṭi. Similarly, nahutaṃ, ninnahutaṃ, akkhobhiṇī, bindu, abbudaṃ, nirabbudaṃ, ahahaṃ, ababaṃ, aṭaṭaṃ, sogaṇḍikaṃ, uppalaṃ, kumudaṃ, puṇḍarīkaṃ, padumaṃ, kathānaṃ, mahākathānaṃ, and asaṅkhyeyya should be understood in order as being one hundred lakh times the preceding number.

Iccevaṃ ṭhānato ṭhānaṃ, satalakkhaguṇaṃ mataṃ;

Koṭippabhutīnaṃ vīsa-saṅkhyānañca yathākkamanti.

Thus, from one place to the next, it is reckoned as a hundred lakh times; and from koṭi onwards, there are twenty numbers in order.

Athā+saṃkhyā vuccate, abyayanti ca vuccate. Taṃ pādi cādi, upasagganipātāti ca duvidhaṃ.

Now indeclinables (asaṅkhyā) are spoken of; they are also called abyaya. They are twofold: the group beginning with pa (prefixes) and the group beginning with ca (particles).

Pa parā apa saṃ anu ava o ni du vi adhi api ati su u abhi pati pari upa ā ime vīsati pādayo. Pādayo hi jotakā, na vācakā.

These twenty are the prefixes (pādayo): pa, parā, apa, saṃ, anu, ava, o, ni, du, vi, adhi, api, ati, su, u, abhi, pati, pari, upa, ā. For prefixes are indicators, not primary denoters of meaning.

Tattha pa-saddo pakārā+dikamma, padhāna+ntobhāva, viyoga, tappara, bhusattha, sambhava, titti, anāvila, patthanādīsu. Yathā pakāre-paññā. Ādikamme-vippakataṃ, padhāne-paṇītaṃ, antobhāve-pakkhittaṃ, khittanti peraṇaṃ, pakkhittanti antokaraṇaṃ, dhātvatthassa bādhitattā. Vutthañhi –

Among these, the prefix pa is used in the senses of manner, beginning, excellence, inclusion, separation, devotion, abundance, origin, satisfaction, purity, aspiration, and so on. For example: in the sense of manner—paññā (wisdom); in the sense of beginning—vippakataṃ (begun); in the sense of excellence—paṇītaṃ (excellent); in the sense of inclusion—pakkhittaṃ (placed within). Khittaṃ means throwing, whereas pakkhittaṃ means placing within, because the meaning of the root is obstructed. For it has been said:

Dhātvatthaṃ bādhate koci, koci taṃ anuvattate;

Tameva+ñño viseseti, upasaggagatī tidhāti.

One may obstruct the meaning of the root, another may accord with it; yet another may make it more specific—thus, the functions of prefixes are threefold.

Ettha ca “anuruddhakā me saṅgāmayuddhe”ti ca ime upasaggā dhātvatthaṃ visesenti nāma. Viyoge-pavāsī, tappare-pācariyo, bhusatthe-pavuddhakāyo, sambhave-himavantā gaṅgā pabhavati[M 0.0098], tittiyaṃ-pahūta+mannaṃ, anāvile-pasanna+mudakaṃ, patthane-paṇihitaṃ.

And here, in a phrase such as 'anuruddhakā me saṅgāmayuddhe' (my followers in battle), these prefixes are said to specify the meaning of the root. [Continuing examples for pa:] In separation: pavāsī (one who lives abroad). In devotion: pācariyo (a pre-eminent teacher). In the sense of abundance: pavuddhakāyo (one with a greatly developed body). In origin: himavantā gaṅgā pabhavati (the Ganges originates from the Himalayas). In satisfaction: pahūtaṃ annaṃ (abundant food). In purity: pasannaṃ udakaṃ (clear water). In aspiration: paṇihitaṃ (aspired).

Parāiti parihāni, parājaya, gati, vikkamā+masanādīsu. Yathā parihāniyaṃ-parābhavo. Parājaye-parājito, gatiyaṃ-parāyanaṃ, vikkame-parakkamati, āmasane-aṅgassa parāmasanaṃ.

The prefix parā is used in the senses of decline, defeat, movement, exertion, touching, and so on. For example: in decline—parābhavo (ruin); in defeat—parājito (defeated); in movement—parāyanaṃ (the final goal); in exertion—parakkamati (strives); in touching—aṅgassa parāmasanaṃ (touching of a limb).

Apaiti apagata, garaha, vajjana, pūjā, padussanādīsu. Yathā apagate-apamāno apeto, garahe-apagabbho, vajjane-apasālāya āyanti vāṇijā, pūjāyaṃ-vuddhāpacāyī, padussane-aparajjhanti.

The prefix apa is used in the senses of departure, disparagement, avoidance, veneration, offense, and so on. For example: in departure—apamāno apeto (one who has departed from conceit); in disparagement—apagabbho (not arrogant); in avoidance—apasālāya āyanti vāṇijā (merchants come away from the hall); in veneration—vuddhāpacāyī (one who venerates elders); in offense—aparajjhanti (they offend).

Saṃiti samodhāna, sammāsama, samantabhāva, saṃgata, saṃkhepa, bhusattha, saha+ppattha, pabhavā+bhimukhabhāva, vidhāna, punappuna, karaṇa, samiddhādīsu. Yathā samodhāne-sandhi, sammāsame-samādhi, sampayutto, samantabhāve-saṃkiṇṇaṃ, samullapanā, saṃgate-saṅgamo, saṃkhepe-samāso, bhusatthe-sārattho, sahatthe-saṃvāso, appatthe-samaggho, pabhave-sambhavo, abhimukhabhāve-sammukhaṃ. Saṃgate-saṃgaṇhāti, vidhāne-saṃvutaṃ, punappunakaraṇe-sandhāvati, samiddhiyaṃ-sampanno.

The prefix saṃ is used in the senses of conjunction, completeness, universality, togetherness, abbreviation, abundance, association, origination, facing towards, arrangement, repeated action, accomplishment, and so on. For example: in conjunction—sandhi; in completeness—samādhi, sampayutto; in universality—saṃkiṇṇaṃ, samullapanā; in togetherness—saṅgamo; in abbreviation—samāso; in abundance—sārattho; in association—saṃvāso; in the sense of 'little'—samaggho (of little value); in origination—sambhavo; in facing towards—sammukhaṃ; in togetherness—saṃgaṇhāti (gathers); in arrangement—saṃvutaṃ; in repeated action—sandhāvati; in accomplishment—sampanno.

Anuiti anugatā+nupacchinna, pacchāttha, bhusattha, sādissa, hīna, tatiyattha, lakkhaṇi+tthambhūtakkhāna, bhāga, vicchādīsu. Anugate-anveti, anupacchinne-anusayo, pacchātthe-anurathaṃ, bhusatthe-anuratto, sādisse-anurūpaṃ, hīne-anusāriputtaṃ paññavanto, tatiyatthe-nadi+manvavasitā senā, lakkhaṇerukkha+manuvijjotate vijju, itthambhūtakhyāne-sādhu devadatto mātara+manu[M 0.0099], bhāge-ya+dettha maṃ anu siyā, taṃ dīyatu, vicchāyaṃ-rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ anu vijjotate cando.

The prefix 'anu' indicates following, uninterruptedness, subsequent meaning, excessive meaning, similarity, inferiority, the sense of the instrumental case, characteristic, description of a thing's nature, portion, distribution, and so on. For example: in following—'anveti' (follows); in uninterruptedness—'anusayo' (underlying tendency); in subsequent meaning—'anurathaṃ' (according to the chariot); in excessive meaning—'anuratto' (enamored); in similarity—'anurūpaṃ' (suitable); in inferiority—'anusāriputtaṃ paññavanto' (wise in a way inferior to Sāriputta); in the sense of the instrumental case—'nadiṃ anvavasitā senā' (the army encamped along the river); in characteristic—'rukkhaṃ anuvijjotate vijju' (lightning flashes along the tree); in description of a thing's nature—'sādhu devadatto mātaraṃ anu' (Devadatta is virtuous towards his mother); in portion—'yaṃ dettha maṃ anu siyā, taṃ dīyatu' (whatever of it would be my portion, let that be given); in distribution—'rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ anu vijjotate cando' (the moon shines on every tree).

Avaiti adhobhāga, viyoga, paribhava, jānana, suddhi nicchaya, desa, theyyādīsu. Adhobhāge-avakkhittacakkhu, viyoge-avakokilaṃ vanaṃ, paribhave-avajānanaṃ, avamaññati, jānane-avagacchati. suddhiyaṃ–vodānaṃ (rūpasiddhi), Nicchaye-avadhāraṇaṃ, dese-avakāso, theyye-avahāro.

The prefix 'ava' indicates lower part, separation, contempt, knowing, certainty, place, theft, and so on. For example: in lower part—'avakkhittacakkhu' (downcast eyes); in separation—'avakokilaṃ vanaṃ' (a forest without cuckoos); in contempt—'avajānanaṃ' (disdain), 'avamaññati' (despises); in knowing—'avagacchati' (understands); in certainty—'avadhāraṇaṃ' (ascertainment); in place—'avakāso' (opportunity); in theft—'avahāro' (misappropriation).

Oiti oroharaṇa, nīharaṇa, suddhiādīsu dissati. Orohaṇe-pāsādā orohati, nīharaṇe-omukkupāhano, suddhiyaṃ-odātaṃ.

The prefix 'o' is seen in the senses of descending, removing, purity, and so on. For example: in descending—'pāsādā orohati' (descends from the palace); in removing—'omukkupāhano' (one who has removed his shoes); in purity—'odātaṃ' (white).

Niiti, nissesa, niggata, nīharaṇa,+ntopavesanā+bhāva, nisedhana, nikkhanta, pātubhāvā+vadhāraṇa, vibhajana, upamu+padhāraṇā+vasāna, cheka, nīharaṇā+varaṇādīsu. Nissese-nirutti, niggate-nikkileso, niyyāti, nīharaṇe-niddhāraṇaṃ, antopavesane-nikhāto, abhāve-nimmakkhikaṃ, nisedhe-nivāreti, nikkhante-nibbānaṃ, pātubhāve-nimmitaṃ, avadhāraṇe-nicchayo, vibhajane-niddeso. Upamāyaṃ-nidassanaṃ, upadhāraṇe-nisāmanaṃ, avasāne-niṭṭhitaṃ, cheke-nipuṇo, nīharaṇe-nīharati, issa dīgho. Āvaraṇe-nīvaraṇaṃ.

The prefix 'ni' indicates completeness, departure, removal, entering, absence, prohibition, going forth, manifestation, ascertainment, division, simile, consideration, end, cleverness, removal, obstruction, and so on. For example: in completeness—'nirutti' (etymology); in departure—'nikkileso' (without defilements), 'niyyāti' (goes forth); in removal—'niddhāraṇaṃ' (singling out); in entering—'nikhāto' (inserted); in absence—'nimmakkhikaṃ' (without flies); in prohibition—'nivāreti' (restrains); in going forth—'nibbānaṃ' (Nibbāna); in manifestation—'nimmitaṃ' (created); in ascertainment—'nicchayo' (certainty); in division—'niddeso' (explanation); in simile—'nidassanaṃ' (illustration); in consideration—'nisāmanaṃ' (consideration); in end—'niṭṭhitaṃ' (finished); in cleverness—'nipuṇo' (skillful); in removal—'nīharati' (removes), where the 'i' is long; in obstruction—'nīvaraṇaṃ' (hindrance).

Duiti asobhaṇā+bhāva, kucchitā+samiddhi, kiccha, virūpatādīsu. Asobhaṇe-duggandho, abhāve-dubbhikkhaṃ, kucchite – dukkaṭaṃ[M 0.0100]. Asamiddhiyaṃ-dussassaṃ, kicche-dukkaraṃ, virūpatāyaṃ-dubbaṇṇo dummukho.

The prefix 'du' indicates unpleasantness, absence, wickedness, lack of success, difficulty, deformity, and so on. For example: in unpleasantness—'duggandho' (foul smell); in absence—'dubbhikkhaṃ' (famine); in wickedness—'dukkataṃ' (wrong action); in lack of success—'dussassaṃ' (poor harvest); in difficulty—'dukkaraṃ' (hard to do); in deformity—'dubbaṇṇo' (ugly complexion), 'dummukho' (ugly face).

Viiti visesa, vividha, viruddha, vigata, viyoga, virūpatādīsu. Visese-vimutti, visiṭṭho, vividhe-vimati, viruddhe-vivādo, vigate-vimalaṃ, viyoge-vippayutto, virūpatāyaṃ-virūpo.

The prefix 'vi' indicates distinction, variousness, opposition, departure, separation, deformity, and so on. For example: in distinction—'vimutti' (liberation), 'visiṭṭho' (distinguished); in variousness—'vimati' (doubt); in opposition—'vivādo' (dispute); in departure—'vimalaṃ' (stainless); in separation—'vippayutto' (dissociated); in deformity—'virūpo' (deformed).

Adhiiti adhiki+ssarū+paribhāvā+dhibhavana+jjhāyā+dhiṭṭhāna, nicchaya, pāpuṇanādīsu. Adhike-adhisīlaṃ, issare-adhipati, adhi brahmadatte pañcālā, uparibhāve-adhirohati, pathaviṃ adhisessati, adhibhavane-adhibhavati, ajjhāyane-byākaraṇa+madhīte, adhiṭṭhāne-bhūmikampādiṃ adhiṭṭhāti, nicchaye-adhimokkho, pāpuṇane-bhogakkhandhaṃ adhigacchati.

The prefix 'adhi' indicates surpassing, lordship, superiority, mastery, study, resolve, determination, attainment, and so on. For example: in surpassing—'adhisīlaṃ' (higher virtue); in lordship—'adhipati' (overlord), 'adhi brahmadatte pañcālā' (the Pañcālas are under Brahmadatta); in being upon—'adhirohati' (ascends), 'pathaviṃ adhisessati' (lies upon the earth); in mastery—'adhibhavati' (overcomes); in study—'byākaraṇaṃ adhīte' (studies grammar); in resolve—'bhūmikampādiṃ adhiṭṭhāti' (resolves upon an earthquake, etc.); in determination—'adhimokkho' (resolution); in attainment—'bhogakkhandhaṃ adhigacchati' (attains a mass of wealth).

Apiiti sambhāvanā+pekkhā, samuccaya, garaha, pañhādīsu. Sambhāvanāyaṃ-api dibbesu kāmesu, merumpi vinivijjhitvā gaccheyya, apekkhāyaṃ-ayampi dhammo aniyato, samuccaye-itipi arahaṃ, antampi antaguṇampi ādāya, garahe-api amhākaṃ paṇḍitaka, pañhe-api bhante bhikkhaṃ labhittha.

The particle 'api' indicates possibility, expectation, accumulation, censure, questions, and so forth. In possibility: 'api dibbesu kāmesu' (even in divine pleasures), 'merumpi vinivijjhitvā gaccheyya' (one might even pierce Mount Meru and go through). In expectation: 'ayampi dhammo aniyato' (this Dhamma too is uncertain). In accumulation: 'itipi arahaṃ' (he is also an Arahant), 'antampi antaguṇampi ādāya' (taking even the end and the quality of the end). In censure: 'api amhākaṃ paṇḍitaka' (oh, our little scholar!). In questions: 'api bhante bhikkhaṃ labhittha' (Venerable Sir, did you receive alms?).

Atiiti atikkamanā+tikkantā+tisaya, bhusatthādīsu. Atikkame-atirocati amhehi, atīto, atikkante-accantaṃ, atisaye-atikusalo, bhusatthe-atikodho, ativuddhi.

The prefix 'ati' indicates exceeding, being past, excess, intensity, and so forth. For example: in exceeding—'atirocati amhehi' (he surpasses us), 'atīto' (past); in the sense of having gone beyond—'accantaṃ' (exceedingly); in excess—'atikusalo' (exceedingly skilled); in intensity—'atikodho' (excessive anger), 'ativuddhi' (overgrowth).

Suiti sobhaṇa, suṭṭhu, sammā, samiddhi, sukhatthādīsu. Sobhaṇe-sugandho, suṭṭhu+sammādatthesu-suṭṭhu gato sugato, sammā [M 0.0101] gatotipi sugato, samiddhiyaṃ-subhikkhaṃ, sukhatthe-sukaro.

The prefix 'su' indicates excellence, well, rightly, prosperity, ease, and so forth. In excellence: 'sugandho' (fragrant). In the sense of 'well' and 'rightly': 'suṭṭhu gato sugato' (well-gone is Sugata), 'sammā gatotipi sugato' (rightly gone is also Sugata). In prosperity: 'subhikkhaṃ' (plentiful food). In the sense of ease: 'sukaro' (easy to do).

Uiti uggatu+ddhakamma, padhāna, viyoga, sambhava, attalābha, satti, sarūpakathanādīsu. Uggate-uggacchati, uddhakamme-āsanā uṭṭhito, ukkhepo, padhāne-uttamo, lokuttaro, viyoge-ubbhāsito, sambhave-ubbhuto, attalābhe-uppannaṃ ñāṇaṃ, sattiyaṃ-ussahati gantuṃ, sarūpakathane-uddisati suttaṃ.

The prefix 'u' indicates rising, upward action, pre-eminence, separation, origin, acquisition, power, description of nature, and so forth. In rising: 'uggacchati' (it rises). In upward action: 'āsanā uṭṭhito' (risen from a seat), 'ukkhepo' (lifting up). In pre-eminence: 'uttamo' (supreme), 'lokuttaro' (supramundane). In separation: 'ubbhāsito' (shone forth). In origin: 'ubbhuto' (born). In acquisition: 'uppannaṃ ñāṇaṃ' (knowledge has arisen). In power: 'ussahati gantuṃ' (one strives to go). In description of nature: 'uddisati suttaṃ' (one indicates a sutta).

Abhiiti abhimukhabhāva, visiṭṭhā+dhiku+ddhakamma, kula, sāruppa, vandana, lakkhaṇi+tthambhūtakkhāna, vicchādīsu. Abhimukhabhāve-abhimukho, abhikkamati, visiṭṭhe-abhidhammo, adhike-abhivasati, uddhakamme-abhiruhati. Kule-abhijāto, sāruppe-abhirūpo, vandane-abhivādeti, lakkhaṇādīsu purimasamaṃ.

The prefix 'abhi' indicates facing, distinction, excess, upward action, lineage, suitability, reverence, and also has the senses of characteristic, description of a thing's nature, distribution, and so forth. For example: in facing—'abhimukho' (facing), 'abhikkamati' (approaches); in distinction—'abhidhammo' (the higher Dhamma); in excess—'abhivasati' (dwells with mastery); in upward action—'abhiruhati' (ascends); in lineage—'abhijāto' (well-born); in suitability—'abhirūpo' (handsome); in reverence—'abhivādeti' (pays respects); in characteristics, etc.: as before.

Patiiti paṭigata, paṭiloma, paṭinidhi, paṭidāna, nisedha, nivattana, sādissa, paṭikaraṇā+dāna, paṭibodha, paṭicca, lakkhaṇitthambhūtakkhāna, bhāga, vicchādīsu. Paṭigate-paccakkhaṃ, paṭilome-paṭisotaṃ, paṭinidhimhi-ācariyato pati sisso, paṭidāne-telatthikassa ghataṃ paṭidadāti, nisedhe-paṭisedheti, nivattane-paṭikkamati, sādisse-paṭirūpakaṃ, paṭikaraṇe-paṭikāro, ādāne-paṭiggaṇhāti, paṭibodhe-paṭivedho, paṭicce-paccayo, lakkhaṇādīsu purimasamaṃ.

The prefix 'paṭi' indicates going back, reversing, substitution, giving back, prohibition, turning back, similarity, reparation, receiving, understanding, conditionality, and also has the senses of characteristic, description of a thing's nature, portion, distribution, and so forth. In going back: 'paccakkhaṃ' (directly perceptible). In reversing: 'paṭisotaṃ' (against the stream). In substitution: 'ācariyato paṭi sisso' (a student instead of a teacher). In giving back: 'telatthikassa ghataṃ paṭidadāti' (one gives ghee to one seeking oil). In prohibition: 'paṭisedheti' (one prohibits). In turning back: 'paṭikkamati' (one turns back). In similarity: 'paṭirūpakaṃ' (a likeness). In reparation: 'paṭikāro' (reparation). In receiving: 'paṭiggaṇhāti' (one receives). In understanding: 'paṭivedho' (penetration). In conditionality: 'paccayo' (condition). In characteristics, etc.: as before.

Pariiti samantatobhāva, pariccheda, vajjanā+liṅgana, nivasana, pūjā, bhojanā+vajānana, dosakkhāna, lakkhaṇādīsu. Samantha- tobhāve-parivuto[M 0.0102], paricchede-pariññeyyaṃ, vajjane-pariharati, āliṅgane-parissajati, nivasane-yo vatthaṃ paridahessati, pūjāyaṃ-paricariyā, bhojane-bhikkhuṃ parivisati, avajānane-paribhavati. Dosakkhāne-paribhāsati, lakkhaṇādīsu-rukkhaṃ pari vijjotate vijju iccādi.

The prefix 'pari' indicates all-aroundness, delimitation, avoidance, embracing, dressing, worship, eating, contempt, fault-finding, characteristics, and so forth. For example: in all-aroundness—'parivuto' (surrounded); in delimitation—'pariññeyyaṃ' (to be fully understood); in avoidance—'pariharati' (one avoids); in embracing—'parissajati' (one embraces); in dressing—'yo vatthaṃ paridahessati' (he who will wear the robe); in worship—'paricariyā' (attendance); in eating—'bhikkhuṃ parivisati' (one serves the monk); in contempt—'paribhavati' (one despises); in fault-finding—'paribhāsati' (one reproaches); in characteristics, etc.—'rukkhaṃ pari vijjotate vijju' ('lightning illuminates around the tree'), and so forth.

Upaiti upagamana, samīpū+papatti, sādissā+dhiku+paribhāvā+nasana, dosakkhāna, saññā, pubbakamma, pūjā, gayhākāra, bhusatthādīsu. Upagamane-nisinnaṃ vā upanisīdeyya, samīpe-upanagaraṃ, upapattiyaṃ-saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati, atha vā upapatti=yutti, yathā upapattito ikkhatīti upekkhā, sādisse-upamānaṃ, upamā, adhike-upakhāriyaṃ doṇo, uparibhāve-upasampanno, anasane-upavāso, dosakkhāne-paraṃ upavadati, saññāyaṃ-upadhā, upasaggo, pubbakamme-upakkamo, upakāro, pūjāyaṃ-buddhupaṭṭhāko, mātupaṭṭhānaṃ, gayhākāre-soceyyapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, bhusatthe-upādānaṃ, upāyāso, upanissayoti.

The prefix 'upa' indicates approach, proximity, rebirth or suitability, similarity, excess, superiority, fasting, fault-finding, designation, prior action, worship, manner of grasping, intensity, and so forth. For example: in approach—'nisinnaṃ vā upanisīdeyya' (one should sit near one who is seated); in proximity—'upanagaraṃ' (near a town); in rebirth or suitability—'saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati' (one is reborn into a heavenly world), or 'upapatti' means appropriateness, as in 'upapattito ikkhatīti upekkhā' (one who sees appropriately is equanimous); in similarity—'upamānaṃ' (comparison), 'upamā' (simile); in excess—'upakhāriyaṃ doṇo' (a doṇa measure less than a khāri); in superiority—'upasampanno' (accomplished); in fasting—'upavāso' (fasting); in fault-finding—'paraṃ upavadati' (one blames another); in designation—'upadhā' (penultimate letter), 'upasaggo' (prefix); in prior action—'upakkamo' (attempt), 'upakāro' (favor); in worship—'buddhupaṭṭhāko' (attendant on the Buddha), 'mātupaṭṭhānaṃ' (attending on one's mother); in manner of grasping—'soceyyapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ' (the presence of purity); in intensity—'upādānaṃ' (clinging), 'upāyāso' (distress), 'upanissayo' (strong dependence).

Āiti abhimukhabhāvu+ddhakamma+mariyādā+bhividhi, patti+cchā, parissajana, ādikamma, gahaṇa, nivāsana, samīpa, āvhānādīsu. Abhimukhabhāve-āgacchanti, uddhakamme-ārohati, mariyādāyaṃ-āpabbatā khettaṃ, abhividhimhi-ākumāraṃ yaso kaccāyanassa, pattiyaṃ-āpattiṃ āpanno, icchāyaṃ-ākaṅkhā, parissajane-āliṅganaṃ, ādikamme-ārambho, gahaṇe-ādīyati, āliṅgati, (ālimpati, rū), nivāse-āvasatho, āvāso, samīpe-āsannaṃ, āvhāne-āmanteti.

Ā is used in the sense of facing, upward action, boundary, extent, attainment, desire, embracing, beginning, taking, dwelling, proximity, summoning, and so forth. In facing: they come. In upward action: one ascends. In boundary: the field extends up to the mountain. In extent: the fame of Kaccāyana extends up to the boys. In attainment: one has fallen into an offense. In desire: longing. In embracing: embracing. In beginning: beginning. In taking: one takes, one embraces. In dwelling: dwelling, abode. In proximity: near. In summoning: one summons.

Pa [M 0.0103] parā+pa sa+manva+va, o ni du rabhi byā+dhisu;

Ati ni ppati pari apayo, upa ā iti vīsati;

Esa hi bho upasagga-vidhi+kkamato kathito.

Pa, Parā, Apa, Saṃ, Anu, Ava, O, Ni, Du, Abhi, Vi, Ā, Adhi, Su; Ati, Ni, Pati, Pari, Apa, Upa. These are twenty. This, indeed, good sir, is the explanation of prefixes, told in order.

Ettha ca –

Herein also:

Upasagga+nipātā ca, paccayā ca ime tayo;

Neke+nekatthavācakā, iti neruttikā+bravuṃ.

Prefixes, particles, and suffixes, these three, have many and diverse meanings; thus the etymologists have said.

118. Asaṃkhyehi sabbāsaṃ

118. Of all countless (forms).

Avijjamānasaṃkhyehi parāsaṃ sabbāsaṃ vibhattīnaṃ lopo hoti. Na santi ekavacanādisaṃkhyā etesanti asaṃkhyā, tesaṃ asaṃkhyānaṃ vibhattīnaṃ bhede asatipi syādividhānaṃ “mā no ajja vikantiṃsū”tiādo vibhatyantattā padattasiddhīti vo+noādīnaṃ siddhiyā ca tesaṃ paṭhamādiatthe dassanato ca hoti. Pahāro parābhavo apahāro saṃhāro avahāro ohāro iccādi hoti.

Elision occurs for all inflections of others by means of non-existent numbers. There are no singular, etc., numbers for these, hence they are 'countless.' Even in the absence of distinctions among these countless inflections, the formation of 'sya,' etc., occurs, such as in "mā no ajja vikantiṃsū"—because the status of a word is established by the inflectional ending. This is also due to the establishment of 'vo,' 'no,' etc., and the explanation of their meaning as first case, etc. Striking, ruin, removal, gathering, carrying away, abandoning—and so on—occur.

Upecca+tthaṃ sajantīti, upasaggā hi pādayo;

Cādī padādimajjhante, nipātā nipatantīti.

Having approached the meaning, they attach themselves, thus they are prefixes (upasagga), indeed, pa and so forth; particles (nipāta), such as ca, fall at the beginning, middle, or end of words, and are thus so called.

Opasaggikapadaṃ.

The Section on Prefixes.

Samuccaya+vikappana+paṭisedha+pūraṇādiatthaṃ asattavācikaṃ nepātikaṃ.

The indeclinable, having meanings such as collection, alternative, negation, and completion, does not denote a substance.

Ca-iti samuccayā+nvācaya+itaretarayoga+samāhārā+vadhāraṇādīsu. Vā-iti vikappanu+pamāna+samuccaya+vavatthitavibhāsādīsu. Na, no, mā, a, alaṃ, halaṃ iccete paṭisedhe[M 0.0104]. “Dve paṭisedhā pakatiatthaṃ gamayantī”ti ñāyā “na tesaṃ pana rūpānaṃ paccayā na ca hontī”ti ettha na ca na honti-hontevāti pakatiatthaṃ gamayati. Alaṃ pariyatti+bhūsanesu ca.

Ca—in the sense of collection, sequence, mutual connection, aggregation, emphasis, etc. Vā—in the sense of alternative, comparison, collection, determination, optional meanings, etc. Na, no, mā, a, alaṃ, halaṃ—these are used for negation. By the principle, "Two negations convey the natural meaning," in "But for those forms, there are no causes, nor do they come to be," the phrase "na ca na honti" (nor do they not come to be) conveys the natural meaning, that is, "they do indeed come to be." Alaṃ—also in the sense of sufficiency and embellishment.

Pūraṇatthaṃ duvidhaṃ attapūraṇaṃ padapūraṇañca, tattha atha, khalu, vata, atho, assu, yagghe, hi, carahi, naṃ, taṃ, ca, tu, vā, vo, pana, have, kīva, ha, tato, yathā, sudaṃ, kho, ve, haṃ, enaṃ, (evaṃ, rū) seyyathidaṃ iccevamādi padapūraṇe. Tattha atha-iti pañhā+nantariyā+dhikārādīsu ca. Khalu-iti paṭisedhā+vadhāraṇa, pasiddhīsu ca. Vata+iti ekaṃsa, khedā+nukampa, saṃkappesu ca. Atho-iti anvādese ca. Hi-iti hetu, avadhāraṇesu ca. Tu-iti visesa, hetu, nivattanādīsu ca. Pana-iti visesepi. Have+ve iccete ekaṃsatthepi. Haṃ-visāda, vimhesupi. (Visāda, sambhavesu, rū). Seyyathidaṃti taṃ katamaṃti atthepi.

Expletives are of two kinds: meaning-fillers (atthapūraṇa) and word-fillers (padapūraṇa). Among these, atha, khalu, vata, atho, assu, yagghe, hi, carahi, naṃ, taṃ, ca, tu, vā, vo, pana, have, kīva, ha, tato, yathā, sudaṃ, kho, ve, haṃ, enaṃ, (evaṃ, rū) seyyathidaṃ, and so on, are word-fillers. Among these, atha is also used in questions, immediacy, and introducing a topic, etc. Khalu is also used in negation, emphasis, and well-known facts. Vata is also used in certainty, sorrow, compassion, and resolve. Atho is also used in subsequence. Hi is also used in reason and emphasis. Tu is also used in distinction, reason, and turning away, etc. Pana is also used in distinction. Have and ve are also used in the sense of certainty. Haṃ is also used in dejection and bewilderment. Seyyathidaṃ is also used in the sense of "what is that?".

Atthapūraṇaṃ duvidhaṃ vibhattiyuttaṃ avibhattiyuttañca. Atthi, sakkā, labbhā iccete paṭhamāyaṃ. Āvuso ambho hambho are hare re je iccete āmantaṇe. Divā bhiyyo (namo, rū) iccete paṭhamādutiyāsu. Sayaṃ sāmaṃ saṃ sammā kinti iccete tatiyatthe. So+to+dhāpaccayantā ca suttaso padaso aniccato dukkhato ekadhā dvidhā iccādi. Tave+tuṃ paccayantā catutthiyāva, kātave dātave, kātuṃ kāretuṃ, (dātuṃ, rū) dāpetuṃ iccādi. So+topaccayantā pañcamiyatthe, dīghaso oraso rājato vā corato vā iccādi. To satta- myatthepi [M 0.0105] tra+tthādipaccayantā ca, ekato purato pacchato passato piṭṭhito pādato sīsato aggato mūlato, yatra yattha yahiṃ tatra tattha tahiṃ iccādi. Samantā sāmantā parito abhito samantato ekajjhaṃ ekamantaṃ heṭṭhā upari uddhaṃ adho tiriyaṃ sammukhā paramukhā āvi raho tiro uccaṃ nīcaṃ anto antarā antaraṃ ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā bāhirā bāhiraṃ bahi oraṃ pāraṃ ārā ārakā pacchā pure huraṃ pecca iccete sattamiyā. Sampati āyati ajja aparajjha suve sve uttarasuve (kisu, rū) hiyyo pare (parasuve, rū) sajju sāyaṃ pāto kālaṃ kallaṃ divā rattaṃ niccaṃ satataṃ abhiṇhaṃ abhikkhaṇaṃ muhuṃ muhuttaṃ bhūtapubbaṃ purā yadā tadā (kadā, rū) iccādayo kālasattamiyaṃ. Iti vibhattiyuttāni.

Meaning-fillers are of two kinds: those connected with case endings and those unconnected with case endings. Atthi, sakkā, labbhā, etc.—these are in the first case. Āvuso, ambho, hambho, are, hare, re, je, etc.—these are in the vocative. Divā, bhiyyo, (namo, rū), etc.—these are in the first and second cases. Sayaṃ, sāmaṃ, saṃ, sammā, kinti, etc.—these are in the sense of the third case. Also those ending with the suffixes so, to, and dhā, such as suttaso, padaso, aniccato, dukkhato, ekadhā, dvidhā, etc. Those ending with the suffixes tave and tuṃ are in the fourth case, such as kātave, dātave, kātuṃ, kāretuṃ, (dātuṃ, rū), dāpetuṃ, etc. Those ending with the suffixes so and to are in the sense of the fifth case, such as dīghaso, oraso, rājato vā, corato vā, etc. To is also in the sense of the seventh case, as are those ending with the suffixes tra, ttha, and others, such as ekato, purato, pacchato, passato, piṭṭhito, pādato, sīsato, aggato, mūlato, yatra, yattha, yahiṃ, tatra, tattha, tahiṃ, etc. Samantā, sāmantā, parito, abhito, samantato, ekajjhaṃ, ekamantaṃ, heṭṭhā, upari, uddhaṃ, adho, tiriyaṃ, sammukhā, paramukhā, āvi, raho, tiro, uccaṃ, nīcaṃ, anto, antarā, antaraṃ, ajjhattaṃ, bahiddhā, bāhirā, bāhiraṃ, bahi, oraṃ, pāraṃ, ārā, ārakā, pacchā, pure, huraṃ, pecca, etc.—these are in the seventh case. Sampati, āyati, ajja, aparajjha, suve, sve, uttarasuve, (kisu, rū), hiyyo, pare, (parasuve, rū), sajju, sāyaṃ, pāto, kālaṃ, kallaṃ, divā, rattaṃ, niccaṃ, satataṃ, abhiṇhaṃ, abhikkhaṇaṃ, muhuṃ, muhuttaṃ, bhūtapubbaṃ, purā, yadā, tadā, (kadā, rū), etc.—these are in the temporal seventh case. Thus, those connected with case endings.

Avibhattiyuttesu appeva appevanāma nu iccete saṃsayatthe. Addhā aññadatthu taggha jātu kāmaṃ sasakkaṃ iccete ekaṃsatthe. Evaṃ iti avadhāraṇe. Kacci nu nanu kathaṃ (kiṃsu, rū) kiṃ iccete pucchanatthe. Evaṃ iti itthaṃ iccete nidassanatthe. Iti hetu+vākyaparisamattīsu ca. Yāva tāva yāvatā tāvatā kittāvatā ettāvatā kīva iccete paricchedanatthe. Evaṃ sāhu lahu opāyikaṃ paṭirūpaṃ āma sādhu iccete sampaṭicchanatthe. Tathā yathā yatheva tatheva evaṃ evameva evampi yathāpi seyyathāpi seyyathāpināma viya iva yathariva tathariva yathānāma tathānāma yathāhi tathāhi yathāca tathāca iccete paṭibhāgatthe. Yathāiti yoggatā+vicchā+padatthānativatti+nidassanesu ca. Evaṃiti [M 0.0106] upadesa+pañhādīsu ca. Kiñcāpiiti anuggahatthe. Dhiiti garahe. Ahoiti garaha+pasaṃsana+patthanesu. Nāmaiti garaha+pasaṃsana+saññā+pañhesu. Sādhūti pasaṃsana+yācanesu. Iṅgha handa iccete codanatthe. Sādhu suṭṭhu evametaṃti anumodane. Kiraiti anussavana+asaddheyyesu. Nunaiti anumānā+nussaraṇa+parivitakkesu. Kasmāti kāraṇapucchane. Yasmā tasmā tathā hi tena iccete kāraṇacchedanatthe. Saha saddhiṃ amā (samaṃ, rū) iti samakriyāyaṃ. Vinā rite vippayoge. Nānā puthu bahupakāre. Puthu visuṃ asaṅghāte ca. Duṭṭhu ku kucchāyaṃ (jigucchāyaṃ, rū). Puna appaṭhame. Kathaṃ cikicchatthe. Dhā kkhattuṃ so kiñcaiti saṃkhyāvibhāge. Īsakaṃ appamānesu (appamatte, rū). Saṇikaṃ mandatthe. Khippaṃ araṃ lahuṃ āsu tuṇhaṃ aciraṃ sīghatthe. Ciraṃ cirassaṃ dīghakāle. Ce yadi saṃkā+vaṭṭhāne. Dhuraṃ thirā+vadhāraṇesu (dhuvaṃ thirā+vadhāraṇesu, rū). Hā visāde. Tuṇhī abhāsane. Sacchi paccakkhe. Musā micchāalikaṃ asacce. Suvatthi āsiṭṭhe iccādi.

Among those unconnected with case endings, appeva, appevanāma, and nu are in the sense of doubt. Addhā, aññadatthu, taggha, jātu, kāmaṃ, and sasakkaṃ are in the sense of certainty. Evaṃ and iti are in the sense of emphasis. Kacci, nu, nanu, kathaṃ, (kiṃsu, rū), and kiṃ are in the sense of questioning. Evaṃ, iti, and itthaṃ are in the sense of illustration. Iti is also used for cause and the conclusion of a sentence. Yāva, tāva, yāvatā, tāvatā, kittāvatā, ettāvatā, and kīva are in the sense of limitation. Evaṃ, sāhu, lahu, opāyikaṃ, paṭirūpaṃ, āma, and sādhu are in the sense of acceptance. Tathā, yathā, yatheva, tatheva, evaṃ, evameva, evampi, yathāpi, seyyathāpi, seyyathāpināma, viya, iva, yathariva, tathariva, yathānāma, tathānāma, yathāhi, tathāhi, yathāca, and tathāca are in the sense of comparison. Yathā is also used in the senses of suitability, wishing, non-transgression of the word's meaning, and illustration. Evaṃ is also used in instruction, questioning, etc. Kiñcāpi is in the sense of concession. Dhi is in the sense of reproach. Aho is used for reproach, praise, and wishing. Nāma is used for reproach, praise, designation, and questioning. Sādhu is used for praise and requesting. Iṅgha and handa are in the sense of urging. Sādhu, suṭṭhu, and evametaṃ are in the sense of approval. Kira is used for hearsay and disbelief. Nuna is used for inference, recollection, and consideration. Kasmā is for questioning the reason. Yasmā, tasmā, tathā hi, and tena are for explaining the reason. Saha, saddhiṃ, and amā (samaṃ, rū) are in the sense of joint action. Vinā and rite are in the sense of separation. Nānā and puthu are in the sense of variety. Puthu and visuṃ are also in the sense of non-aggregation. Duṭṭhu and ku are in the sense of disgust. Puna is in the sense of 'not first'. Kathaṃ is in the sense of hesitation. Dhā, kkhattuṃ, so, and kiñca are in the sense of numerical division. Īsakaṃ is in the sense of a small amount. Saṇikaṃ is in the sense of slowness. Khippaṃ, araṃ, lahuṃ, āsu, tuṇhaṃ, and aciraṃ are in the sense of quickness. Ciraṃ and cirassaṃ are in the sense of a long time. Ce and yadi are in the sense of doubt and condition. Dhuraṃ (dhuvaṃ, rū) is in the sense of firmness and emphasis. Hā is in the sense of dejection. Tuṇhī is in the sense of silence. Sacchi is in the sense of 'directly'. Musā, micchā, and alikaṃ are in the sense of falsehood. Suvatthi is in the sense of a blessing, etc.

Tuna+ktvāna+ktvāpaccayantā ussukkanatthe bhavanti. Yathā passituna passiya passitvāna passitvā, disvā disvāna dassetvā dātuna datvāna datvā upādāya dāpetvā viññāya viceyya vineyya samecca nihacca upecca ārabbha āgamma iccādi.

Words ending in the suffixes tuna, ktvāna, and ktvā are in the sense of the absolutive. For example: passituna, passiya, passitvāna, passitvā (all meaning 'having seen'); disvā, disvāna ('having seen'); dassetvā ('having shown'); dātuna, datvāna, datvā ('having given'); upādāya ('having taken up'); dāpetvā ('having caused to give'); viññāya ('having understood'); viceyya ('having investigated'); vineyya ('having removed'); samecca ('having met/understood'); nihacca ('having struck down'); upecca ('having approached'); ārabbha ('having begun'); āgamma ('having come'); and so on.

Vibhattiyā [M 0.0107] kato bhedo, saliṅgānaṃ bhave tathā;

Tumhādīnaṃ tva+liṅgesu, neva+tthi pādi+cādinaṃ.

A distinction is made by case-ending, and likewise for those with gender; for `tumha` and so on, in the three genders, there are not the groups of indeclinables beginning with `pā` and `ca`.

Evaṃ nāmākhyātopasaggehi vinimuttaṃ etaṃ nipātapadaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Thus, this indeclinable word should be understood as being distinct from nouns, verbs, and prefixes.

Nepātikapadaṃ.

The Section on Indeclinables.

Pulliṅgaṃ itthiliṅgañca, napuṃsaka+mathā+paraṃ;

Tiliṅgañca aliṅgañca, nāmikaṃ pañcadhā ṭhitaṃ.

Masculine gender, feminine gender, and then the neuter gender; that which is of three genders, and that which is genderless—the nominal word thus stands in five ways.

Iti payogasiddhiyaṃ nāmakaṇḍo dutiyo.

Thus ends the second chapter, the Chapter on Nouns, in the Payogasiddhi.

3. Kārakakaṇḍa

3. The Chapter on Kāraka.

Atha [M 0.0108] vibhattīna+matthabhedā vuccante.

Now, the distinctions in the meanings of the case endings are stated.

Tattha ekampi atthaṃ kammādivasena ekattādivasena ca vibhajantīti vibhattiyo, syādayo. Tā pana paṭhamādibhedena sattavidhā. Tā yathā “paṭhamā+tthamatte”ti paṭhamāvibhatti hoti. Sissa okāra+lopa+a-mādesesu naro itthī napuṃsakaṃ.

In this context, the case endings (`vibhattiyo`), such as `si` and so forth, are so called because they analyze even a single meaning by way of syntactic role (`kamma`), etc., and by way of number, such as singularity, etc. They are, however, sevenfold, distinguished as the first and so on. For example, the first case ending (`paṭhamāvibhatti`) occurs in the mere meaning of the stem. For the suffix `si`, through the operations of its change to `o`, its elision, and its substitution by `aṃ`, the forms `naro`, `itthī`, and `napuṃsakaṃ` are derived.

Sakattha+dabba+liṅgāni, saṃkhyā+kammādipañcakaṃ;

Nāmattho tassa sāmañña-matthamatthaṃ pavuccate.

Its own meaning, substance, gender, number, and the fivefold set beginning with `kamma`—this is the meaning of a noun. Its generality, the mere meaning, is called 'meaning'.

So nāmattho ca –

And that meaning of a noun is—

Jāti kriyā guṇo dabbaṃ, tathā nāmanti pañcadhā;

Saddassa+ttho sa saddopi, pañcadhāva+tra bhijjate.

Class, action, quality, substance, and name—thus fivefold is the meaning of a word. And that word itself is also divided fivefold here.

Kathaṃ jātisaddo guṇasaddotyādinā.

How is a word for class distinguished from a word for quality, and so forth?

Bhinnesva+bhinnadhī+saddā, sabalādīsu yabbalā;

Vattante jāti esā+ssa, mālā sutta+mivā+nvitā.

That by which, in distinct things, an undivided perception and a single word operate, as in the case of spotted cows and so on, that is class (`jāti`), pervading them like a thread through a garland.

Adabbabhūtaṃ kattādi-kārakaggāmasādhiyaṃ;

Padatthaṃ kattukammaṭṭhaṃ, kriya+micchanti tabbidū.

That which is not a substance, which is to be accomplished by the collection of kārakas beginning with the agent, and which is the meaning of a word residing in the agent and the object—that, those who know it call 'action' (`kriyā`).

Dabbassito tato bhinno, nimitto tappatītiyā;

Vinassanasabhāvo ca, nigguṇova guṇo+ccate.

That which resides in a substance, is distinct from it, is the cause of its perception, and has a perishable nature, is called a quality (`guṇa`), though it is itself devoid of qualities.

Ettha [M 0.0109] paṭo sukkoti vinassanasabhāvo ca casaddena vipulo ākāsoti avinassanasabhāvo ca attani visuṃ guṇarahito guṇo+ccate tyattho.

Here, 'the cloth is white' (`paṭo sukko`) refers to that which has a perishable nature; and by the word `ca` (and), 'the sky is vast' (`vipulo ākāso`) refers to that which has an imperishable nature. The meaning is that a quality (`guṇa`) is so called even though it is itself separate and devoid of qualities.

Yaṃ yaṃ visessate kiñci, taṃ taṃ dabba+miho+ccate;

Jātyādinopya+to tādi, dabbattaṃ parikappate.

Whatever is in any way distinguished, that is called 'substance' (`dabba`) here. Therefore, even class and so on, when they are likewise distinguished, are conceived of as having the nature of a substance.

Ettha gojāti assajātīti vutte jāti dabbaṃ. Nīlo guṇoti ca guṇo dabbaṃ. Pacanakriyāti ca gamanādikriyāto visesiyatīti kriyāva dabbaṃ.

Here, when 'cow-class' (`gojāti`) and 'horse-class' (`assajāti`) are spoken of, class (`jāti`) is the substance. And when 'blue is a quality' (`nīlo guṇo`) is spoken of, quality (`guṇa`) is the substance. And in the case of 'the action of cooking' (`pācanakriyā`), because it is distinguished from actions like going and so on, action (`kriyā`) itself is the substance.

Nāmarūpena sadabbe, kvaci saññī kathīyate;

Nāmanti taṃ yathā citto, saññā saddo tu taddhanī.

In a substance having name and form, that which is designated (`saññī`) is sometimes spoken of. That designation is called 'name' (`nāma`), as for example 'Citta'. The designating word (`saññā saddo`), however, is the possessor of that designation.

Nāmassa dabbattepi cittotyādi nāmeneva pasijjhati, no ghaṭa+paṭādayova dabbattena, tasmā nāma+miti saññī kathīyate, taṃvācakattā tabbatī cittādi saññāsaddoti nicchiyateyya+dhippāyo.

Although a name has the nature of a substance, 'Citta' and so on are established by the name itself, not like pots, cloths, and so on, by their substantiality. Therefore, 'name' (`nāma`) is called the designated entity (`saññī`). The intention is that because it is the designator of that entity, a word like 'Citta' is to be determined as a designating word (`saññāsadda`).

Ayaṃ pañcavidhopi attho saddattho ceva sāmatthiyā gamyamānattho cāti dubbidho. Tathā hi “pīno divā na bhuñjeyya”miti bhuttinirākati saddattho. Rattibhutti tu sāmatthiyā+vagamyate. Tene+taṃ vuccati –

This fivefold meaning is also twofold: the literal meaning of the word (`saddattho`) and the meaning understood by implication (`sāmatthiyā gamyamānattho`). For example, in the sentence, 'A fat person should not eat during the day' (`pīno divā na bhuñjeyya`), the rejection of eating during the day is the literal meaning. But eating at night is understood by implication. Therefore, it is said—

Atthappatītiyaṃ sadda-byāpāro tividho bhave;

Mukhyo lakkhaṇa+byañjana-sabhāvo cāti ettha tu.

In the comprehension of meaning, the function of a word may be threefold: of a primary, indicative, and suggestive nature.

Mukhyo tu nirantaratthe, lakkhaṇo tu tirohite;

Atthe+taro tu vākyassa, attheyeva pavattati.

The primary function relates to the direct meaning, the indicative to the concealed meaning; the other, however, operates in the meaning of the sentence itself.

“Mañce”ti [M 0.0110] nirantaratthe vattamāno mukhyo, “mañcā ugghosantī”ti tirohitatthe vattamāno lakkhaṇo, gāthādisakalavākyassa+tthe vattamāno byañjanasabhāvo.

'On the bed' (`mañce`), operating in the direct sense, is primary. 'The beds are shouting' (`mañcā ugghosanti`), operating in the concealed sense, is indicative. The suggestive nature is that which operates in the meaning of an entire sentence, such as a verse and so on.

Byāpārassa pabhedena, tidhā saddopi vācako;

Lakkhaṇiko byañjakoti, tadatthopi tidhā mato.

By the division of its function, the word is also threefold: designative (`vācako`), indicative (`lakkhaṇiko`), and suggestive (`byañjako`). Its meaning is likewise considered threefold.

Vacco lakkhaṇiko byaṅgyo, cevaṃ saddo suvācako;

Vuttakamena jātyādi-bhedena pañcadhā bhaveti.

The expressed (`vacca`), the indicated (`lakkhaṇika`), and the suggested (`byaṅgya`)—thus the word is an effective designator. In the order previously stated, this meaning becomes fivefold through the distinctions of class and so on.

38. Āmantaṇe –

38. In the case of addressing (`āmantaṇa`)—

Ti āmantaṇādhike atthamatte paṭhamāvibhatti hoti. Bho nara, bho itthi, bho napuṃsaka.

Thus, the first case ending occurs in the mere meaning of the stem when there is the additional sense of addressing. For example: 'O man,' 'O woman,' 'O neuter one.'

Saddenā+bhimukhīkāro, vijjamānassa vatthuno;

Āmantaṇaṃ vidhātabbe, natthi “rājā bhave”ti+daṃ.

The act of turning a present object towards oneself by means of a word is addressing (`āmantaṇa`). It is not to be found in the injunctive, such as in 'May you be king' (`rājā bhave`).

Kriyā nimittaṃ kārakantu kamma, kattu, karaṇa, sampadāna, avadhi, ādhārabhedena chabbidhaṃ, taṃ yathā –

Action is the distinguishing mark; the kāraka, however, is sixfold, distinguished by object, agent, instrument, recipient, source, and location. For example:

2,2. Kamme dutiyā

2.2. The Second Case Ending: The Object

Karīyati kattukiriyāya sambandhīyatīti kammaṃ, tasmiṃ kammakārake dutiyāvibhatti hoti. Taṃ tividhaṃ nibbatti, vikati, patti bhedena, tattha nibbattikamme mātā puttaṃ vijāyati, āhāro sukhaṃ janayati, kaṭaṃ karoti datto. Vikatiyaṃ kaṭṭha+maṅgāraṃ karoti, suvaṇṇaṃ kaṭakaṃ karoti, vīhayo lunāti. Pattiyaṃ datto gharaṃ pavisati, ādiccaṃ passati, dhammaṃ suṇāti, paṇḍite payirupāsati.

That which is done, that which is related to the action of the agent, is the object. In that kāraka of the object, the second case ending occurs. It is threefold by distinction of production, modification, and attainment. Therein, in the production-object: a mother gives birth to a son, food produces happiness, Datta makes a mat. In the modification-object: one makes wood into charcoal, one makes gold into a bracelet, one harvests rice. In the attainment-object: Datta enters a house, sees the sun, hears the Dhamma, attends upon the wise.

Vuttañca [M 0.0111] –

And it is said:

Nibbatti+vikati+patti-bhedā kammaṃ tidhā mataṃ;

Kattukriyābhigammantaṃ, sukha+maṅgāraṃ+gharaṃ yathāti.

The object is considered threefold by the distinctions of production, modification, and attainment; it is that which is reached by the action of the agent, like happiness, charcoal, and a house.

Kaṭaṃ karoti vipulaṃ dassanīyanti attheva guṇayuttassa kammatā, vipulaṃ karoti, dassanīyaṃ karotīti kriyāya sambandhiyamānattā. Odano paccateti odanasaddato kammatā nappatīyate, kiñcarahi ākhyātato.

In the sense of 'one makes a mat large and beautiful,' the quality of being an object belongs to that which is endowed with attributes, because it is related to the action, as in 'one makes it large, one makes it beautiful.' In 'rice is cooked' (odano paccati), the quality of being an object is not understood from the word 'rice,' but rather from the verb.

Icchitakammaṃ yathā-gāvuṃ payo dohati, gomantaṃ gāvaṃ yācati, gāva+mava rundhati vajaṃ, māṇavakaṃ maggaṃ pucchati, gomantaṃ gāvaṃ bhikkhate, rukkha+mavacināti phalāni, rukkhātyattho. Sissaṃ dhammaṃ brūte. Ettha payo, gāvaṃ iccādi icchitaṃ, gāvuṃ, gomanta+miccādi anicchitaṃ. Eva+manicchitepi kaṇṭakaṃ maddati, visaṃ gilati. Yaṃ nevi+cchitaṃ, nāpi anicchitaṃ, tatrāpi gāmaṃ gacchanto rukkhamūla+mupasappati.

Regarding the desired object, for example: one milks milk from a cow; one asks for a cow from a cowherd; one confines a cow in a pen; one asks a student the way; one begs for a cow from a cowherd; one picks fruits from a tree (the meaning is 'from the tree'); one teaches the Dhamma to a pupil. Here, 'milk,' 'a cow,' and so on are the desired objects; 'the cow,' 'the cowherd,' and so on are the undesired objects. Likewise, even with an undesired object: one crushes a thorn, one swallows poison. Where something is neither desired nor undesired, there also: while going to the village, one approaches the foot of a tree.

Ādhāre adhisi+ṭhā+sānaṃ payoge ca, pathaviṃ adhisessati, gāma+madhitiṭṭhati, rukkha+majjhāsateti. Ettha pathavinti pathaviyanti attho. Eva+mabhi, nipubbavisassāpi, dhamma+mabhinivisate, dhamme vā. Tathā upa, nva+jjhā+pubbavasatissa, gāma+mupavasati, gāma+manuvasati, vihāra+madhivasati, gāma+māvasati, agāraṃ ajjhavasati, ettha gāmanti gāmetyattho. Tathā tappānā+cārepi, nadiṃ pibati, gāmaṃ carati, nadiyaṃtyattho. Sace maṃ nālapissatīti mayā saddhiṃtyattho. Vihitāva paṭi-yogepi dutiyā, paṭibhantu taṃ cunda bojjhaṅgā, tampaṭi bojjhaṅgā bhāsantūti attho. Upamā maṃ patibhāti[M 0.0112], upamā maṃ upaṭṭhātityattho. Dhātunāyutte “tassa nappaṭibhātī”ti chaṭṭhī.

And in the use of 'adhi' with 'sī' (to lie), 'ṭhā' (to stand), and 'ās' (to sit) in the sense of location: 'one lies upon the earth' (pathaviṃ adhisessati), 'one stands in the village' (gāmaṃ adhitiṭṭhati), 'one sits upon the tree' (rukkhaṃ ajjhāsate). Here, 'pathaviṃ' means 'on the earth' (pathaviyaṃ). Similarly, also with 'vis' preceded by 'abhi' and 'ni': 'one is devoted to the Dhamma' (dhammaṃ abhinivisate), or 'in the Dhamma' (dhamme). Likewise, with 'vas' preceded by 'upa,' 'anu,' 'adhi,' and 'ā': 'one dwells near the village' (gāmaṃ upavasati), 'one dwells in the village' (gāmaṃ anuvasati), 'one dwells in the monastery' (vihāraṃ adhivasati), 'one dwells in the village' (gāmaṃ āvasati), 'one inhabits the house' (agāraṃ ajjhāvasati). Here, 'gāmaṃ' means 'in the village' (gāme). Similarly, also in the sense of drinking and wandering: 'one drinks from the river' (nadiṃ pibati), 'one wanders in the village' (gāmaṃ carati); the meaning is 'in the river' (nadiyaṃ). In 'if he will not speak to me' (sace maṃ nālapissati), the meaning is 'with me' (mayā saddhiṃ). The accusative is also prescribed in conjunction with 'paṭi': 'May the enlightenment factors appear to you, Cunda' (paṭibhantu taṃ cunda bojjhaṅgā); the meaning is 'may the enlightenment factors shine upon you' (taṃ paṭi bojjhaṅgā bhāsantu). 'A simile appears to me' (upamā maṃ paṭibhāti); the meaning is 'a simile presents itself to me' (upamā maṃ upaṭṭhāti). When the verb 'paṭibhāti' is used, it takes the genitive case: 'tassa nappaṭibhāti' (it does not appear to him).

3. Kāladdhāna+maccantasaṃyoge

3. In continuous connection with time and distance.

Kāladdhānaṃ dabba+guṇa+kriyāhi accantasaṃyoge tehi kāladdhānavācīhi dutiyā hoti. Kāle-sattāhaṃ gavapānaṃ, māsaṃ maṃsodanaṃ, saradaṃ ramaṇīyā nadī, sabbakālaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ nandanaṃ, tayo māse abhidhammaṃ deseti. Addhani-yojanaṃ vanarāji, yojanaṃ dīgho pabbato, kosaṃ sajjhāyati.

When there is a continuous connection of time and distance with substance, quality, and action, the accusative case occurs with those words denoting time and distance. In terms of time: 'for seven days, gavapānaṃ,' 'for a month, meat and rice,' 'throughout autumn, the river is delightful,' 'Nandana is always delightful,' 'he teaches the Abhidhamma for three months.' In terms of distance: 'a forest range a yojana long,' 'a mountain a yojana long,' 'he recites for a kosa.'

Pubbanhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā, ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā, imaṃ rattiṃ cattāro mahārājānoti evamādīsu kālavācīhi accantasaṃyoge dutiyā, bahulaṃvidhānā vibhattivipallāso vā. Māsenā+nuvāko+dhīto, kosenā+nuvāko+dhītoti karaṇatthe tatiyā.

In expressions such as 'having dressed in the forenoon,' 'at one time the Blessed One,' 'this night, the four great kings,' and so on, the accusative case is used with words denoting time due to the rule of continuous connection, or it is an interchange of case endings due to extensive usage.

4. Gatibodhāhārasaddatthākammakabhajjādīnaṃ payojje

4. In the causative of verbs of motion, understanding, eating, sounding, intransitive verbs, and those like 'bhajja'.

Gatyatthānaṃ bodhatthānaṃ āhāratthānaṃ saddatthāna+makammakānaṃ bhajjādīnañca payojje kattari dutiyā hoti. Datto gamayati māṇavakaṃ gāmaṃ, yāpayati vā. Guru bodhayati māṇavakaṃ dhammaṃ, vedayati vā. Mātā bhojayati putta+modanaṃ, āsayati vā. Guru ajjhāpayati sissaṃ vedaṃ, pāṭhayati vā. Payojjato+ññatra kamme dutiyā. Poso āsayati dattaṃ, sāyayati vā. Poso aññaṃ bhajjāpeti, aññaṃ koṭṭāpeti, aññaṃ santharāpeti.

In the causative of verbs with the meaning of motion, understanding, eating, sounding, intransitive verbs, and those like 'bhajja,' the accusative case is used for the agent of the original action. For example: Datta makes the young man go to the village, or causes him to go. The teacher makes the young man understand the Dhamma, or causes him to know. The mother feeds the son rice, or causes him to eat. The teacher makes the student study the Veda, or causes him to recite. The accusative case is also used for the object, in addition to the agent of the original action. A man makes Datta eat, or causes him to taste. A man makes another divide, makes another pound, makes another spread.

5. Harādīnaṃ vā

5. Optionally with verbs like 'hara'.

Harādīnaṃ [M 0.0113] payojje kattari dutiyā hoti vā. Poso hāreti bhāraṃ dattaṃ, datteneti vā. Dassayate janaṃ rājā, janeneti vā. Abhivādayate guruṃ dattaṃ, datteneti vā. Ajjhohāreti sattuṃ dattaṃ, datteneti vā. Kāreti datto dattaṃ, datteneti vā. Pakkhe sabbatra kattari tatiyā.

In the causative of verbs like 'hara,' the accusative case is optionally used for the agent of the original action. For example: A man makes Datta carry the burden, or [has it carried] by Datta. The king makes the people see, or [shows] by the people. One makes Datta greet the teacher, or [has the teacher greeted] by Datta. One makes Datta swallow the flour, or [has it swallowed] by Datta. Datta makes another Datta do something, or [has it done] by Datta. In the alternative case, the instrumental is used for the agent everywhere.

6. Na khādādīnaṃ

6. Not with verbs like 'khād'.

Khādādīnaṃ payojje kattari dutiyā na hoti. Gatyatthādīsu kvaci paṭisedhattha+midaṃ. Khādayati datto dattena, ādayati dattena, avhāpayati datthena, saddāyayati dattena, nāyayati dattena, kandayati dattena.

In the causative of verbs like 'khād,' the accusative case is not used for the agent of the original action. This rule is for the purpose of prohibiting in some cases what was stated for verbs of motion, etc. For example: One causes someone to eat by means of Datta, to take by means of Datta, to call by means of Datta, to make a sound by means of Datta, to lead by means of Datta, or to cry by means of Datta.

7. Jhādīhi yuttā

7. In connection with 'dhi' and so forth.

Dhiādīhi yuttato dutiyā hoti. Dhi+ratthu+maṃ putikāyaṃ, antarā ca rājagahaṃ antarā ca nālandaṃ, rājagahassa ca nālandassa ca vivarabhūte majjheti attho. Samādhāna+mantarena, mucalinda+mabhito saraṃ. Chaṭṭhyatthe+yaṃ dutiyā.

The accusative case occurs when connected with 'dhi' and so forth. For example: 'Fie upon me, this foul body!' 'Between Rājagaha and Nālanda,' meaning, in the middle, being the space between Rājagaha and Nālanda. 'Without concentration.' 'Around the lake Mucalinda.' Here, this accusative case is in the sense of the genitive case.

8. Lakkhaṇitthambhūtavicchāsva+bhinā

8. With 'abhi' in the sense of characteristic, state, and repetition.

Lakkhaṇādīsva+tthesu abhinā yuttamhā dutiyā hoti. Rukkha+mabhivijjotate cando, ettha rukkho lakkhaṇaṃ, cando lakkhitabbo, tatra abhinā rukkhassa lakkhaṇavuttitā pakāsīyatīti rukkho abhinā yutto nāma. Sādhu devadatto mātara+mabhi, mātari sādhuttaṃ pattotyattho. Rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃabhi vijjotate cando, rukkhe rukkhetyattho.

The accusative case occurs when connected with 'abhi' in the senses of characteristic and so forth. For example: 'The moon shines upon the tree.' Here, the tree is the characteristic, and the moon is that which is to be characterized; there, by 'abhi,' the tree's function as a characteristic is revealed, thus the tree is said to be 'connected with abhi.' 'Devadatta is good towards his mother,' meaning he has attained goodness with respect to his mother. 'The moon shines upon tree after tree,' meaning upon each tree.

9. Patiparīhi bhāge ca

9. With 'pati' and 'pari' in the senses above, and in the sense of a portion.

Patiparīhi [M 0.0114] yuttato lakkhaṇādīsu bhāge ca+tthe dutiyā hoti. Rukkhaṃpati vijjotate, sādhu devadatto mātaraṃpati, rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃpati tiṭṭhati, ya+dettha maṃ pati siyā, yo mama bhāgo, so dīyatutyattho. Evaṃ rukkhaṃparityādipi.

The accusative case occurs when connected with 'pati' and 'pari' in the sense of characteristic and so forth, and also in the sense of a portion. For example: 'The moon shines upon the tree,' 'Devadatta is good towards his mother,' 'He stands by tree after tree,' 'whatever here might fall to my share, let that be given.' Likewise with 'pari' and so forth.

10. Anunāti

10. With 'anu'.

Lakkhaṇādīsu dutiyā. Rukkhamanu vijjotate, saccakiriya+manu vassi, hetu ca lakkhaṇaṃ bhavati, sādhu devadatto mātara+manu, rukkhaṃ rukkha+manu vijjotate, yadettha maṃanu siyā.

The accusative case is used in the sense of characteristic and so forth. For example: 'The moon shines along the tree,' 'it rained in accordance with the act of truth'—and here the cause becomes the characteristic. 'Devadatta is good towards his mother,' 'the moon shines along tree after tree,' 'whatever here might fall to my share.'

11. Sahatthe

11. In the sense of 'together with'.

Sahatthe anunā yuttamhā dutiyā. Pabbata+manu tiṭṭhati, pabbatena saha tyattho.

The accusative case occurs when connected with 'anu' in the sense of 'together with'. For example: 'He stands along the mountain,' meaning 'with the mountain'.

12. Hīne

12. In the sense of inferiority.

Hīnatthe anunā yuttamhā dutiyā. Anusāriputtaṃ paññavanto bhikkhū, sāriputtato paññāya hīnātyattho.

The accusative case occurs when connected with 'anu' in the sense of inferiority. For example: 'The wise monks are inferior to Sāriputta,' meaning 'they are inferior to Sāriputta in wisdom.'

13. Upena

13. With 'upa'.

Hīnatthe upena yuttamhā dutiyā. Upasāriputtaṃ paññavanto.

The accusative case occurs when connected with 'upa' in the sense of inferiority. For example: 'The wise are inferior to Sāriputta.'

16. Kattukaraṇesu tatiyā

16. The instrumental case is used for agents and instruments.

Kattari karaṇe ca kārake tatiyā hoti. Jinena desito dhammo, buddhena jito māro, ahinā daṭṭho naro. Yattha [M 0.0115] kāraṇakāraṇampi kāraṇavasena vuccati, tatthāpi tatiyā, corehi gāmo daḍḍho, tiṇehi bhattaṃ siddhaṃ, saddhehi kāritā vihārā.

The instrumental case occurs for the agent and the instrument among the kārakas. For example: 'The Dhamma was taught by the Conqueror,' 'Māra was conquered by the Buddha,' 'a man was bitten by a snake.' Where even the cause of the instrument is spoken of in terms of instrumentality, there too the instrumental case is used: 'The village was burned by thieves,' 'the food was cooked with grass,' 'the monasteries were built by those with faith.'

Attapadhāno kiriyaṃ, yo nibbatteti kārako;

Apayutto payutto vā, sa kattāti pavuccati.

The kāraka who, being primary, brings about the action, whether unengaged or engaged, is called the agent.

Karaṇe-taṃ pana duvidhaṃ ajjhattikabāhiravasena, yathā hatthena kammaṃ karoti, cakkhunā rūpaṃ passati, manasā dhammaṃ viññāyati. Dattena vihayo lunāti, agginā kuṭiṃ jhāpeti.

Regarding the instrument, it is twofold, by way of internal and external. For example: one does work with the hand, sees forms with the eye, and cognizes phenomena with the mind. One reaps rice with a sickle, and burns a hut with fire.

Bāhirañca tathā+jjhattaṃ, karaṇaṃ duvidhaṃ yathā;

Vīhiṃ lunāti dattena, nettena canda+mikkhate.

External and likewise internal, the instrument is twofold, as follows: One reaps rice with a sickle, one sees the moon with the eye.

Pakatiyā abhirūpo, gottena gotamo iccādi bhūdhātussa sambhavā karaṇe tatiyā. Tathā sāriputtoti nāmena vissuto, jātiyā khattiyo buddho, jātiyā sattavassiko, sippena naḷakāro so, ekūnatiṃso vayasā, evaṃ samena dhāvati, visamena dhāvati, dvidoṇena dhaññaṃ kiṇāti.

Handsome by nature, Gotama by clan, etc. — in the sense of origin with respect to the root 'bhū', the instrumental case is used. Likewise, renowned by the name Sāriputta; the Buddha, a khattiya by birth; seven years old by birth; he is a reed-worker by craft; twenty-nine years old by age. Thus he runs evenly, he runs unevenly; he buys grain with two doṇas.

17. Sahatthena

17. In the sense of 'with'

Sahatthena yoge tatiyā siyā. Tatiyāpi chaṭṭhīva appadhāne eva bhavati. Puttena sahā+gato, puttena saddhiṃ āgato, vitakkena saha vattati, puttena saha thūlo, nisīdi bhagavā saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena, sahassena samaṃ mitā, sabbehi me piyehi manāpehi nānābhāvo.

In connection with 'saha' (with) and its synonyms, the instrumental case may occur. The instrumental case also, like the genitive, occurs only in a subordinate sense. He went with his son; he came together with his son; it proceeds with thought; he is stout with his son; the Blessed One sat together with the community of monks; equal to a thousand; separation from all my dear and beloved ones.

18. Lakkhaṇe

18. In the sense of a characteristic

Lakkhaṇe [M 0.0116] vattamānato tatiyā. Bhinnena sīsena paggharantena lohitena paṭīvissake ujjhāpesi, ūnapañcabandhanena pattena aññaṃ navaṃ pattaṃ cetāpeyya, tidaṇḍakena paribbājaka+maddakkhi, akkhinā kāṇo, hatthena kuṇī, pādena khañjo, piṭṭhiyā khujjo. Tena hi vikalaṅgena vikalaṅgino vikāro lakkhiyate.

The instrumental case occurs when indicating a characteristic. With a broken head, with blood oozing, he caused the neighbors to complain; with a bowl lacking five bindings, he would have another new bowl obtained; he saw an ascetic with a three-pronged staff; blind in one eye; crippled in hand; lame in foot; hunchbacked. Thus, by means of a defective feature, the defect of the defective person is indicated.

19. Hetumhi

19. In the sense of cause

Vāsādilakkhaṇakriyāya hetuto tatiyā. Annena vasati, vijjāya vasati, na jaccā vasalo hoti, kammunā vasalo hoti, dānena bhogavā, ācārena kulaṃ, tena pāṇi kāmadado.

The instrumental case occurs as a cause for actions such as dwelling. He lives by food; he lives by knowledge; not by birth is one an outcast, by action is one an outcast; wealthy by giving; a family is known by conduct; thereby the hand is a giver of desires.

20. Pañcamī+ṇe vā

20. In the sense of debt, the ablative case is used optionally.

Iṇe hetumhi pañcamī vā. Satasmā baddho, satena vā.

In a cause that is a debt, the ablative case is used optionally. Bound because of a hundred, or by a hundred.

21. Guṇe

21. In the sense of a quality

Paraṅgabhūte hetumhi pañcamī hoti vā. Jaḷattā baddho, jaḷattenavā, paññāya mutto, hutvā abhāvato aniccā, saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho. Bahulaṃvidhānā sattamyatthehipi, tena samayena, kālena dhammasākacchā, puratthimena dhataraṭṭho, dakkhiṇena virūḷhako, uttarena kapilavatthu, yena bhagavā, tenupasaṅkami, so vo mama+ccayena satthāti. Māsena bhuñjati, ekāheneva bārāṇasiṃ pāvisi, navahi māsehi vihāraṃ kārāpesi[M 0.0117], kahāpaṇena ūno, dhanena vikalo, asinā kalaho, ācārena nipuṇo, guḷena missakaṃ, vācāya sakhilo, maṇinā attho, dhanena attho, yojanena gacchati iccādi hetumhi karaṇe vā tatiyā. Attanāva attānaṃ sammannatīti paccatte bahulaṃvidhānā kattari tatiyā. Evaṃ tilehi khette vapatīti kammatthe, sumuttā mayaṃ tena mahāsamaṇenāti pañcamyatthe ca.

When the cause is subordinate, the ablative case may occur. Bound by dullness, or by dullness; freed by wisdom; impermanent due to having ceased to be; with the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness. Due to various application, the instrumental is also used in the senses of the locative. At that time; a discussion of Dhamma in due course; Dhataraṭṭha in the east; Virūḷhaka in the south; Kapilavatthu in the north; where the Blessed One was, there he approached; 'He is your teacher after my passing.' He eats in a month; in a single day, he entered Bārāṇasī; in nine months, he had a monastery built; less by a kahāpaṇa; deficient in wealth; a quarrel with a sword; skilled in conduct; mixed with molasses; friendly in speech; a need for a gem; a need for wealth; he goes by a league—thus, in the sense of cause or instrument, the instrumental case is used. One appoints oneself by oneself—thus, in the reflexive sense, due to various application, the instrumental case is used for the agent. Thus, he sows a field with sesame seeds—in the sense of the object. 'We are well freed by that great ascetic'—and in the sense of the ablative case.

24. Catutthī sampadāne

24. The dative case is used for the recipient (sampadāna).

Acetanaṃ sacetanaṃ vā paṭiggāhakabhāvenā+pekkhitaṃ, taṃ sampadānaṃ, tañca dā-dāneti dhātuto byappena yuttameva, tattha catutthī hoti. Tañca dīyamānassa vatthuno anivāraṇa+jjhesanā+numatito tividho, yathā buddhassa pupphaṃ deti, bodhirukkhassa jalaṃ deti, yācakassa dhanaṃ deti, bhikkhūnaṃ dānaṃ deti.

That which is intended as a recipient, whether inanimate or animate, is the recipient (sampadāna). And that is indeed connected by derivation from the root 'dā' in the sense of 'dāna' (giving). There, the dative case occurs. And that recipient is threefold, based on non-prevention, requesting, and approval of the object being given: as when one offers flowers to the Buddha, gives water to the Bodhi tree, gives wealth to a beggar, or gives alms to the monks.

Anirākaraṇā+rādha-na+bbhanuññavasena hi;

Sampadānaṃ tidhā vuttaṃ, rukkha+yācaka+bhikkhavo.

Indeed, by way of non-rejection, entreaty, and permission, the recipient is said to be threefold: trees, supplicants, and monks.

Ādhāravivakkhāyaṃ sattamīpi, saṅghe gotami dehi, saṅghe dinne ahañceva pūjito bhavissāmi, yā palālamayaṃ mālaṃ, nārī datvāna cetiyeti.

When the basis is intended, the locative case is also used, as in: 'Give to the Sangha, Gotami; when something is given to the Sangha, I myself will be honored.' And: 'A woman, having given a garland made of straw, is esteemed.'

25. Tādatthye

25. In the sense of 'for that purpose'

Tādatthye catutthī siyā. Tadatthassa bhāve, tādatthyaṃ, tasmiṃ tadatthabhāve jotanīyeva catutthī siyā. Tadatthassa bhāvoti nimittanimittīsambandhe [M 0.0118] chaṭṭhī, tasmā chaṭṭhāpavādo+yaṃ. Samepi nimittanimittīnaṃ sambandhe nimittabhūtayūpatova catutthī, no nimittībhūtadāruto. Yūpāya dāru, pākāya vajati, buddhassatthāya jīvitaṃ pariccajāmi, neva davāya, na madāya, ūnassa pāripūriyā, atthāya hitāya sukhāya saṃvattati, lokānukampāya, phāsu vihārāya.

In the sense of 'for that purpose' (tādatthya), the dative case may occur. When there is the state of being for that purpose, that is 'tādatthya'; and to express that state of purpose, the dative case may indeed occur. 'The state of being for that purpose' refers to the relation of cause and effect, for which the genitive case is used; therefore, this is an exception to the genitive case. Even when there is a relation of cause and effect, the dative case applies to the purpose, not to the material from which it is made. For example: wood for a sacrificial post; he goes for cooking; I give up my life for the sake of the Buddha; not for sport, not for intoxication; for the fulfillment of what is lacking; it conduces to welfare, benefit, and happiness; out of compassion for the world; for a comfortable dwelling.

Iccāyaṃ kaccāyane upari vakkhamānassa catutthīti sādhitattā idha chaṭṭhīti dīpanatthaṃ vuccate –

Thus, since it has been established in the Kaccāyana grammar that the dative case is for the words to be mentioned below, here the genitive case is stated for the purpose of explanation—

Kassa sādu naruccati, mā ayasmantānampi saṅghabhedo ruccittha, khamati saṅghassa, bhatta+massa nacchādetīti chaṭṭhī sambandhavacanicchāyaṃ, na ce+vaṃ virodho siyā, sadisarūpattā, evaṃvidhesu ca sambandhassa saddikānumatattā. Tathā hi bhāgavuttiyā “upapadavibhatti chaṭṭhiyā+pavādā”ti vuttaṃ, saddantare vihitā vibhatti upapadavibhatti.

To whom is what is pleasant not pleasing? May schism in the Sangha not be pleasing even to the venerable ones. It is acceptable to the Sangha. The food does not satisfy him—this is the genitive case when desiring to express relation. And thus there is no contradiction, due to the similarity of form, and because in such cases, the relation is acknowledged by grammarians. Thus, in the Bhāgavutti, it is said: 'A case ending determined by a governing word is an exception to the genitive case.' A case ending prescribed in relation to another word is a case ending determined by a governing word.

Kassa vā tvaṃ dhammaṃ rocesīti atthamatte paṭhamā, kassa vā tuyhanti avatvā kassa vā tvaṃ dhammaṃ rocesīti atthamatte paṭhamāvasena byabhicāradassanā. Eva+maññāpi viññeyyā, paratopi yathāgamaṃ.

In 'Whose Dhamma do you approve of?', the nominative case is used in the sense of the mere meaning of the word. A deviation is seen by means of the nominative in the sense of mere meaning in 'Whose Dhamma do you approve of?', as opposed to saying 'Whose are you?'. Thus other instances should also be understood, and also from other sources according to tradition.

Rañño sataṃ dhāreti rañño chattaṃ dhāretīti sambandhe chaṭṭhīva. Silāgha=kathane, evaṃ rañño silāghate iccādi, thutiṃ karotītyattho. Hanu=apanayane, rañño hanute, vañcetītyattho. Upatiṭṭheyya sakyaputtānaṃ vaḍḍhakī, upagaccheyyātyattho. Sapa=akkose, mayhaṃ sapate, saccaṃ kurutetyattho[M 0.0119]. Dhara=dhāraṇe, suvaṇṇaṃ te dhārayate, iṇaṃ te dhārayati, assa rañño nāgaṃ dhārayāma. Piha=icchāyaṃ, devāpi tassa pihayanti tādino, tesaṃ pihayanti sambuddhānaṃ satīmataṃ, pihayanti=patthenti. Tassa kujjha mahāvīra, yadi+haṃ tassa pakuppeyyaṃ, dubhayati disānaṃ megho, yo mittānaṃ na dūbhati, yo appaduṭṭhassa narassa dussati. Issa=issāyaṃ, titthiyā issayanti samaṇānaṃ. Usūya=dosāvikaraṇe, dujjanā guṇavantānaṃ ussūyanti, kā usuyā vijānataṃ. Idha+sidha+rādha+sādha=saṃsiddhiyaṃ, ārādho me rañño, rañño bhāgya+mārajjhati, kyā+haṃ ayyānaṃ aparajjhāmi, āyasmato upālittherassa upasampadāpekkho upatisso. Bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ, āsuṇanti buddhassa bhikkhū, tassa bhikkhuno janoanugiṇāti, patigiṇāti, sādhukāradānādinā taṃ ussahatītyattho. Ārocayāmi vo bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, āmantayāmi te mahārāja, dhammaṃ te desissāmi, desetu bhante bhagavā dhammaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ, yathā no bhagavā byākareyya, niruttiṃ te pavakkhāmi, alaṃ me rajjaṃ, alaṃ bhikkhu pattassa, alaṃ mallo mallassa, arahati mallo mallassa, alaṃ te idha vāsena, kiṃ me ekena tiṇṇenāti sabbattha sambandhe chaṭṭhī.

He owes the king a hundred; he holds the king’s umbrella—this is the genitive in the sense of relation. Silāgha in the sense of speaking: thus, 'He praises the king,' etc., meaning he offers praise. Hanu in the sense of removal: 'He wrongs the king,' meaning he deceives. 'Let the carpenter attend upon the Sakyaputtas,' meaning he should approach. Sapa in the sense of cursing: 'He swears an oath to me,' meaning he makes a vow. Dhara in the sense of bearing: 'He owes you gold'; 'He owes you a debt'; 'Let us hold the elephant for this king.' Piha in the sense of desire: 'Even the gods long for him, such a one'; 'They long for the enlightened, mindful Buddhas'; pihayanti means they desire. 'Be angry with him, O great hero'; 'If I were to become angry with him'; 'The cloud is hostile to both directions'; 'He who does not harm friends'; 'He who wrongs a man who has done no wrong.' Issa in the sense of envy: 'The sectarians envy the ascetics.' Usūya in the sense of revealing faults: 'The wicked find fault with the virtuous'; 'What fault-finding is there for those who understand?' Idha, sidha, rādha, sādha in the sense of accomplishment: 'I have the king's favor'; 'The king’s fortune succeeds'; 'How have I offended the noble ones?'; 'Upatissa, a candidate for higher ordination from the Venerable Upāli Thera.' 'The monks assented to the Blessed One'; 'The monks listen to the Buddha'; 'The people approve of that monk, they accept him,' meaning they encourage him with acclamations of 'Well said!', gifts, and so on. 'I announce to you, O monks'; 'I declare to you'; 'I address you, O great king'; 'I will teach you the Dhamma'; 'May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to the monks'; 'As the Blessed One would explain to us'; 'I will speak the wording to you'; 'Kingship is enough for me'; 'The bowl is enough for the monk'; 'A wrestler is a match for a wrestler'; 'A wrestler is a match for a wrestler'; 'It is enough for you to dwell here'; 'What use to me is one who has crossed over?'—in all these cases, it is the genitive in the sense of relation.

Evaṃ āyu bhoto hotu, ciraṃ jīvitaṃ, bhaddaṃ, kalyāṇaṃ, atthaṃ, payojanaṃ, kusalaṃ, anāmayaṃ, hitaṃ, patthaṃ, sukhaṃ, sātaṃ, bhoto hotu, sādhu sammuti me tassa, puttassā+vikareyya guyha+matthaṃ, tassa me sakko pāturahosi, tassa pahiṇeyya, bhikkhūnaṃ dūtaṃ pāhesi, kappati samaṇānaṃ āyogo[M 0.0120], ekassa dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vā pahoti, upamaṃ te karissāmi, añjaliṃte paggaṇhāmi, tassa phāsu, lokassa+ttho, namo te purisājañña, sotthi tassa, samattho mallo mallassa, tassa hitaṃ, tassa sukhaṃ, svāgataṃ te mahārājāti sabbattha sambandhe chaṭṭhī.

Thus, may there be long life for you; may there be long life, welfare, good fortune, benefit, purpose, skill, health, advantage, desirability, happiness, and pleasure for you. My consent is for his good. May he reveal the secret matter to his son. Sakka appeared to me for his sake. He should send to him. He sent a messenger to the monks. Exertion is suitable for ascetics. It suffices for one, two, or three. I will make a comparison for you. I raise my joined hands to you. Comfort for him. The world's benefit. Homage to you, O noble man. Well-being for him. A wrestler is a match for a wrestler. His welfare. His happiness. Welcome to you, O great king—in all these cases, it is the genitive in the sense of relation.

26. Pañcamya+vadhismā

26. The Fifth Case: In the Sense of a Point of Separation

Padatthāvadhismā pañcamīvibhatti hoti.

The fifth case ending is used for the point of separation from the object denoted by the word-stem.

Samepya+pagame dvinnaṃ, pubbarūpā ya+daccutaṃ;

Vuccate ta+dapādānaṃ, taṃ calācalato dvidhā;

Yathā+ssā dhāvatā poso, pato, rukkhāphalanti ca.

When two things are near and then separate, the prior form from which there is a departure is called the point of separation (apādāna). It is twofold, as moving and unmoving. For example: a man falls from a running horse, and fruits from a tree.

Tattha calāvadhi dhāvatā assā puriso patati, acalāvadhi pabbatā otaranti vanacārakāti.

Therein, an example of a moving point of separation is: 'A man falls from a running horse.' An example of an unmoving point of separation is: 'Forest-dwellers descend from a mountain.'

Tañca avadhi visayakriyāvisesassa niddiṭṭhattā niddiṭṭhavisayaṃ, yattha apa apagamanakriyaṃ upāttaṃ=ajjhāhaṭaṃ visayaṃ katvā pavattati, taṃ upāttaṃ. Yaṃ kenaci guṇena ukkaṃsiyati, taṃ anumeyyaṃ. Yathā gāmā apenti munayo, nagarā niggato rājā, pāpā cittaṃ nivārenti. Valāhakā vijjotate, kusulato pacatīti. Ettha ca vaḷāhakā nikkhamma, kusulato apanetvāti ca pubbakriyā ajjhāharīyati. Mathurā pāṭaliputtakehi abhirūpāti anumīyati. Vuttañhi –

And that point of separation, because a specific action relating to an object is specified, is termed the 'specified object.' Where the action of departing proceeds by making its object implied or supplied, that is termed the 'implied object.' That which is distinguished by some quality is termed the 'inferred object.' For example: 'The sages depart from the village'; 'The king has gone out from the city'; 'They restrain the mind from evil.' 'It flashes from the clouds'; 'He cooks from the granary.' And here, the prior actions 'having come forth from the clouds' and 'having taken from the granary' are supplied. 'Mathurā is more beautiful than the people of Pāṭaliputta' is inferred. For it has been said:

Niddiṭṭhavisayaṃ kiñci, upāttavisayaṃ tathā;

Anumeyyavisayañceti, tidhā+hu avadhiṃ budhāti.

The specified object, likewise the implied object, and the inferred object—thus the wise declare the point of separation to be threefold.

Bhayahetumhi-corā [M 0.0121] bhayaṃ jāyati, taṇhāya jāyati bhayaṃ, pāpato uttasati, natthi soko kuto bhayaṃ. Akkhātari-upajjhāyā sikkhaṃ gaṇhāti, ācariyamhā adhīto suṇāti vā. Buddhasmā parājenti aññatitthiyā, parājitā bhavantītyattho. Himavatā pabhavati gaṅgā, aciravatiyā pabhavanti kunnadiyo. Urasmā jāto putto, kammato jātaṃ indriyaṃ, upajjhāyā antaradhāyati sisso, mātāpitūhi antaradhārayati putto, nilīyatītyattho. Dūratthayogekīvadūro ito naḷakāragāmo, tato have dūrataraṃ vadanti, gāmato nātidūre, ārakā te moghapurisā imasmā dhammavinayā, ārakā tehi bhagavā dūratova namassanti, addasa dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Antikatthayoge-antikaṃ gāmā, āsannaṃ gāmā, samīpaṃ gāmā. Parimāṇe-ito mathurāya catūsu yojanesu saṃkassaṃ, rājagahato pañcacattālīsayojanamatthake sāvatthi. Kālaparimāṇe-ito ekanavutikappamatthake, ito vassasatasahassassa accayena buddho loke uppajjissati. Pāsādā saṃkameyya, pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā saṃkameyyāti attho, tathā hatthikkhandhā saṃkameyya, abhidhammā pucchanti, abhidhammaṃ sutvāti attho, āsanā vuṭṭhaheyya. Disatthavācīhi yoge-ito sā purimā disā, ito sā dakkhiṇā disā, avīcito yāva bhavaggaṃ, uddhaṃ pādatalā, adho kesamatthakā. Vibhajane-yato paṇītataro vā visiṭṭhataro vā natthi, attadanto tato varaṃ, kiñcāpi dānato sīlaṃ varaṃ, tato mayā bahutaraṃ sutaṃ, sīlameva sutā seyyo. Āratippayoge-ārati virati pāpā, pāṇātipātā [M 0.0122] veramaṇi, adinnādānā paṭivirato, appaṭiviratā musāvādā. Suddhatthayoge-lobhanīyehi dhammehi suddho, mātuto ca pituto ca suddho anupakkuṭṭho. Pamocanatthayoge-parimutto dukkhasmāti vadāmi, mutto+smi mārabandhanā, na te muccanti maccunā, mutto+haṃ+sabbapāsehi. Vivecane-vivicceva kāmehi, vivicca akusalehi dhammehi. Pamāṇatthe-āyāmato ca vitthārato ca yojanaṃ, gambhīrato ca puthulato ca yojanaṃ candabhāgāya parimāṇaṃ, parikkhepato navayojanasataparimāṇo majjhimadeso. Pubbādiyoge-pubbeva me bhikkhave sambodhā, ito pubbe nāhosi, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, tato aparena samayena. Pañhe-kuto+si tvaṃ, kuto bhavaṃ, pāṭaliputtato. Kicchā laddhanti guṇe pañcamī, kicchena me adhigatanti hetumhi karaṇe vā tatiyā, evaṃ thokā mutto, thokena muttoti.

In the sense of a cause of fear: 'Fear arises from thieves'; 'Fear arises from craving'; 'One trembles from evil'; 'Where there is no sorrow, whence fear?' In the sense of a teacher: 'He receives training from the preceptor'; 'He studies under or listens to the teacher.' 'Other sectarians are defeated by the Buddha,' meaning they become defeated. 'The Ganges originates from the Himālaya'; 'Small rivers originate from the Aciravatī.' 'A son is born from the chest'; 'Faculties are born from kamma.' 'The pupil disappears from the preceptor'; 'The son hides from his parents,' meaning he conceals himself. In connection with words denoting distance: 'How far is Naḷakāra village from here?'; 'They say it is indeed farther than that'; 'Not too far from the village'; 'Those foolish men are far from this Dhamma and Discipline'; 'They worship the Blessed One from afar'; 'He saw him coming from afar.' In connection with words denoting proximity: 'Near the village'; 'Close to the village'; 'Adjacent to the village.' In the sense of measurement: 'Saṅkassa is four yojanas from Mathurā'; 'Sāvatthī is forty-five yojanas from Rājagaha.'
