In the sense of time measurement: 'From now, at the end of ninety-one eons'; 'After the passing of a hundred thousand years from now, a Buddha will arise in the world.' 'One may cross over from the palace,' meaning, having ascended the palace, one may cross over. Similarly, 'One may cross over from the elephant's back.' 'They ask questions from the Abhidhamma,' meaning, having heard the Abhidhamma. 'One should rise from the seat.' In connection with words denoting direction: 'From here is the eastern direction'; 'From here is the southern direction'; 'From Avīci up to the peak of existence'; 'Upward from the soles of the feet'; 'Downward from the tips of the hair.' In differentiation: 'Than which there is nothing more refined or more distinguished'; 'A self-tamed person is better than that'; 'Although virtue is better than generosity'; 'I have heard much more than that'; 'Virtue is indeed better than learning.' In connection with abstinence: 'Abstinence and refraining from evil'; 'Abstinence from killing living beings'; 'He has refrained from taking what is not given'; 'Not having refrained from false speech.' In connection with purity: 'Pure from states that entice greed'; 'Pure from the side of his mother and father, unblemished.' In connection with liberation: 'I say he is completely liberated from suffering'; 'I am freed from Māra’s bonds'; 'They are not freed from death'; 'I am freed from all snares.' In seclusion: 'Secluded indeed from sensual pleasures'; 'Secluded from unwholesome states.' In the sense of measure: 'A yojana in length and in breadth'; 'A yojana in depth and in width is the measure of the Candabhāgā'; 'The Middle Country measures nine hundred yojanas in circumference.' In connection with 'before,' etc.: 'Even before my full enlightenment, monks'; 'Before this, it did not exist'; 'Beyond that are the border countries'; 'After that, at another time.' In questions: 'Whence are you?'; 'Whence is the venerable one?'; 'From Pāṭaliputta.' In 'obtained with difficulty,' the fifth case is used for the quality. In 'I attained with difficulty,' the third case is used for the cause or instrument. Thus: 'escaped from a little danger,' and 'escaped by a small margin.'

Kathaṃ “thokaṃ calatī”ti, kriyāvisesane kammani dutiyā, thokaṃ calanaṃ karotītyattho, thokanti calanakriyāya visesanattā kriyāvisesanaṃ.

How is it in 'thokaṃ calati' (he moves a little)? The second case (accusative) is used for an adverbial action in the objective sense, meaning 'he does a little moving.' 'Thokaṃ' is an adverb because it qualifies the action of moving.

Kriyāvisesanaṃ nāma, kammatte+kattasaṇṭhitā;

Nyāyasiddhaṃ yato tasmā, tadatthaṃ na visuṃ vidhi.

An adverb, indeed, is established as an agent in the sense of an object; since it is established by reason, there is therefore no separate rule for its meaning.

Nyāyasiddhaṃva=calananti yasmā bhāve ano, tasmā bhāvasse+kattā ekavacananti ñāyā ekattañca, bhāve anattā napuṃsakattañca, karotikriyāya sambandhena kammattañca sijjhatīti. Kara+bhūdhātavo ca –

It is established by reason, indeed: since in `calana` (moving) the suffix `-ana` denotes a verbal noun, therefore, by the rule that a verbal noun is singular, singularity is established; and since a verbal noun is without gender, the neuter gender is established; and through connection with the action of 'doing', its status as an object is accomplished. And the roots `kar` (to do) and `bhū` (to be)—

Kāriyarūpābhidhātvatthā[M 0.0123], sabbe sattāya yujjare;

Tato kriyā ca bhāvo ca, sāmaññaṃ tesu gamyate –

The meanings of roots that denote forms of action are all connected with existence; thence, action and state of being, and their generality, are understood in them—

Ti vuttattā yujjanti.

Thus, because it is said, they are appropriate.

Thokatthe-thokā muccati. Sabbattha savisaye pañcamī. Ettha “vivakkhā lokikā sā ca, na sakkā anivattituṃ”ti vuttattā aniṭṭhappasaṅgo na siyā. Mariyādāyaṃ-āpabbatā khettaṃ. Abhividhimhi-ābrahmalokā saddo abbhuggacchati, pabbataṃ vajjetvā, brahmalokamhi byāpetvāti ca attho. Ettha vajjamānasīmā mariyādā, gayhamānasīmā abhividhi.

In the sense of 'a little'—'He is freed a little.' Everywhere, the fifth case is used in its own sphere. Here, since it is said, 'And that worldly intention cannot be reversed,' there should be no undesirable consequence. In the sense of limit—the field extends up to the mountain. In the sense of inclusion—the sound arises up to the Brahma world; and the meaning is, 'excluding the mountain' for the limit, and 'pervading the Brahma world' for the inclusion. Here, the excluded boundary is the limit, and the included boundary is the inclusion.

27. Apaparīhi vajjane

27. With `apa` and `pari` in the sense of exclusion.

Vajjane vattamānehī apaparīhi yoge pañcamī hoti. Apasālāya āyanti vāṇijā, parisālāya āyanti vāṇijā, sālaṃ vajjetvāti attho.

When `apa` and `pari` are used in the sense of exclusion, the fifth case occurs. `Apasālāya āyanti vāṇijā`, `parisālāya āyanti vāṇijā`: merchants come, avoiding the hall; the meaning is 'having excluded the hall'.

28. Paṭinidhipatidānesu patinā

28. With `pati` in the sense of substitution and exchange.

Paṭinidhimhi patidāne ca vattamānena patinā yoge nāmasmā pañcamī hoti. Buddhasmā pati sāriputto, ghata+massa telasmā pati dadāti.

When `pati` is used in the sense of substitution and exchange, the fifth case occurs with a noun. Sāriputta is a substitute for the Buddha. He gives ghee in exchange for oil.

29. Rite dutiyā ca

29. With `rite`, and also the second case.

Ritesaddayoge nāmasmā dutiyā hoti pañcamī ca. Rite saddhammā, rite saddhammaṃ.

When the word `rite` is used, the second and fifth cases occur with a noun. Without the True Dhamma (ablative), without the True Dhamma (accusative).

30. Vinā+ññatra tatiyā ca

30. With `vinā` and `aññatra`, and also the third case.

Vinā+ññatrayoge [M 0.0124] nāmasmā tatiyā dutiyā pañcamī ca. Vinā vātena, vinā vātaṃ, vinā vātasmā. Aññatra ekena piṇḍapātanīhārakena, aññatra dhammaṃ, aññatra dhammā.

When `vinā` and `aññatra` are used, the third, second, and fifth cases occur with a noun. Without wind (instrumental), without wind (accusative), without wind (ablative). Except for one alms-gatherer (instrumental), except for the Dhamma (accusative), except for the Dhamma (ablative).

31. Puthanānāhi

31. With `puthu` and `nānā`.

Etehi yoge tatiyā hoti pañcamī ca. Bhinnayogakaraṇaṃ dutiyānivattanatthaṃ. Puthageva janena, puthageva janasmā, janena nānā, janasmā nānā.

When these words are used, the third and fifth cases occur. The separate rule is for the purpose of excluding the second case. Separately from a person (instrumental), separately from a person (ablative); differently from a person (instrumental), differently from a person (ablative).

39. Chaṭṭhī sambandhe

39. The sixth case in the sense of relation.

Sambandhe chaṭṭhī hoti. Rañño purisoti vutte yasmā rājā dadāti, puriso gaṇhāti, tasmā rājapurisoti viññāyati. Evameva yo yassa āyatto sevakādibhāvena bhaṇḍabhāvena vā samīpa+samūhā+vayava+vikāra+kāriya+avatthā+jāti+guṇa+kriyādivasena vā, ṭhānīvasena vā, āgamīvasena vā, so tividhopi attho sambandho nāma. Vuttañhi –

The sixth case occurs in the sense of relation. When 'the king's man' is said, it is understood as 'the king's man' because the king gives and the man receives. Similarly, whoever is dependent on another—whether through being a servant, through being property, or through proximity, collection, part, modification, effect, condition, class, quality, action, and so on, or through location, or through source—this threefold meaning is called 'relation.' For it is said—

Kriyākārakasañjāto, asse+daṃbhāvahetuko;

Sambandho nāma so attho, tattha chaṭṭhī vidhīyate.

Arising from action and agent, caused by the nature of 'this is of that'; that meaning is called relation, wherein the sixth case is prescribed.

Pāratantyañhi sambandho, tattha chaṭṭhī bhave tito;

Upādhi+ṭhānyā+gamito, na visessādito titoti.

Dependence is indeed relation; therein the sixth case arises. It arises from adjunct, location, and source, not from the qualifier and so forth.

Upādhisaṅkhātavisesanato tāva-rañño puriso. Ettha ca brāhmaṇādisāmito nivattetīti rājā visesanaṃ, puriso tena [M 0.0125] visesiyatīti visesso. Bhaṇḍasambandhato-pahutaṃ me dhanaṃ sakka, ekassa paṭivīso, bhikkhussa pattacīvaraṃ. Samīpato-ambavanassa avidūre, nibbānasseva santike. Samūhe-suvaṇṇassa rāsi, bhikkhūnaṃ samūho. Avayave-manussasseva te sīsaṃ, rukkhassa sākhā. Vikāre-suvaṇṇassa vikati, bhaṭṭhadhaññānaṃ sattu. Kāriye-yavassa aṅkuro, meghassa saddo, puttāpi tassa bahavo, kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko. Avatthāyaṃ-khandhānaṃ pātubhāvo, jarā, bhedo vā. Jātiyaṃ-manussassa bhāvo, manussānaṃ jāti. Guṇe-suvaṇṇassa vaṇṇo, vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassa buddhassa guṇaghoso, pupphānaṃ gandho, phalānaṃ raso, cittassa phusanā, sippikānaṃ sataṃ natthi, tilānaṃ muṭṭhi, tesaṃ samāyogo, sandhino vimokkho, tathāgatassa paññāpāramiṃ ārabbha, sukhaṃ te, dukkhaṃ te, cetaso parivitakko udapādi, paññāya paṭubhāvo, rūpassa lahutā, mudutā vā, upacayo vā. Kriyāsambandhe-pādassa ukkhepanaṃ, avakkhepanaṃ vā, hatthassa samiñjanaṃ, dānaṃ, pasāraṇaṃ, dhātūnaṃ gamanaṃ, ṭhānaṃ, nisajjā, sayanaṃ vā, tathāgatassa nāmagottādi, tassa kāraṇaṃ, tassa mātāpitaro, tassa purato pāturahosi, nagarassa dakkhiṇato, vassānaṃ tatiye māse, na tassa upamā, kuverassa bali iccādi. Api ca –

First, from the qualifier designated as an adjunct: 'the king's man'. Here, because it distinguishes him from a master who is a brahmin and so on, 'king' is the qualifier, and 'man', being qualified by it, is the qualified. By relation to possessions—'Much wealth is mine, Sakka,' 'a share for one,' 'a monk’s bowl and robe.' By proximity—'Not far from the mango grove,' 'close to Nibbāna.' By collection—'A heap of gold,' 'an assembly of monks.' By part—'Your head is like a man's,' 'the branch of a tree.' By transformation—'A product of gold,' 'flour from parched grain.' By effect—'A sprout of barley,' 'the sound of a cloud,' 'he has many sons,' 'the result of actions is the ripening.' By state—'The manifestation of the aggregates,' 'aging,' or 'breaking apart.' By class—'The state of being human,' 'the birth of humans.' By quality—'The color of gold'; 'the complexion of the Tathāgata would not fade'; 'the resounding virtue of the Buddha'; 'the fragrance of flowers'; 'the taste of fruits'; 'the mind’s contact'; 'there is not a hundred skilled artisans'; 'a handful of sesame seeds'; 'their combination'; 'the liberation from the bond'; 'concerning the Tathāgata’s perfection of wisdom'; 'happiness is yours'; 'suffering is yours'; 'a thought arose in the mind'; 'the manifestation of wisdom'; 'the lightness of form,' 'its softness,' or 'its increase.' By relation to action—'The lifting of the foot,' or 'the lowering of it'; 'the bending of the hand,' 'giving,' 'stretching out'; 'the movement of elements,' 'standing,' 'sitting,' or 'lying down'; 'the Tathāgata’s name and clan, etc.'; 'its cause'; 'his parents'; 'he appeared before him'; 'south of the city'; 'in the third month of the rains'; 'there is no equal to him'; 'the offering to Kuvera,' and so on. Moreover—

Gāvassa jāti, dhavalo, gati, siṅgaṃ, nāmanti+dha;

Dabbassāpi ca jātyādi, visessā honti kāmato.

A cow's species, white color, gait, horn, and name, here; and also a substance's species etc., become qualifiers as desired.

Gottañca [M 0.0126] sabalodissa, pāka+mannassa sukkatā;

Paṭassa, siṅgaṃmeṇḍassa, nā+ññesaṃti visessate.

And the lineage of a strong bull, the goodness of cooked food, of a cloth, the horn of a ram; these are distinguished thus, not of others.

Ṭhānito-yuvaṇṇāna+meo luttā. Āgamito-suña sassa. Sāmiyoge-devāna+mindo, migānaṃ rājā. Rujādiyoge-devadattassa rujati, tassa rogo uppajji, mahāsenāpatīnaṃ ujjhāpetabbaṃ, rajakassa vatthaṃ dadāti, musāvādassa ottappaṃ iccādi. Yajassa yoge-pupphassa buddhassa yajati, pupphenātyattho. Evaṃ ghatassa aggiṃ juhati. Suhitatthe-pattaṃ odanassa pūretvā, pūraṃ nānāpakārassa asucino, pūraṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇassa, pūrati bālo pāpassa. Kitakappayoge-bahulaṃvidhānā chaṭṭhī, rañño sammato, pūjito, sakkato, apacito, mānito vā, amataṃ tesaṃ bhikkhave aparibhuttaṃ, yesaṃ kāyagatā sati aparibhuttā, sādhusammato bahujanassa, suppaṭividdhā buddhānaṃ dhammadhātu, dhammassa gutto medhāvī. Kammatthe-tassa bhavanti vattāro, sahasā kammassa kattāro, amatassa dātā, bhinnānaṃ sandhātā, sahitānaṃ anuppadātā, bodhetā pajāya, kammassa kārako natthi, vipākassa ca vedako, avisaṃvādako lokassa, catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādo. Sarati+cchāyoge-mātu sarati, na tesaṃ koci sarati, sattānaṃ kammapaccayā, puttassa icchati. Karotissa (yoge) – udakassa patikurute, kaṇḍassa patikurute, abhisaṅkharotītyattho. Pañcamiyatthe parihānibhayatthayogepi chaṭṭhī, assavanatāya dhammassa pariyāyanti, kinnu kho ahaṃ tassa sukhassa bhāyāmi, sabbe tasanti daṇḍassa, sabbe bhāyanti [M 0.0127] maccuno, bhīto catunnaṃ āsīvisānaṃ ghoravisānaṃ iccādi.

From location: 'the wealth of the young was robbed.' From source: 'empty of grain.' In connection with ownership: 'the lord of the gods,' 'the king of beasts.' In connection with `ruj` etc.: 'Devadatta aches,' 'his sickness arose,' 'the great generals should be reproached,' 'he gives cloth to the washerman,' 'shame regarding false speech,' and so on. In connection with `yaj`: 'he worships the Buddha with flowers,' the meaning is 'with flowers.' Thus, 'he offers ghee to the fire.' In the sense of 'filled': 'having filled the bowl with rice,' 'full of various kinds of impurity,' 'full of gold and silver,' 'the fool is filled with evil.' In connection with participles: the sixth case is frequently prescribed: 'approved by the king,' 'worshipped,' 'respected,' 'revered,' or 'honored.' 'The deathless, O monks, is not experienced by those for whom mindfulness of the body is not experienced.' 'Well-regarded by the multitude,' 'the Dharma-element is well-penetrated by the Buddhas,' 'the wise one is protected by the Dhamma.' In the sense of object: 'there are speakers of it,' 'sudden doers of an action,' 'giver of the deathless,' 'reconciler of the divided,' 'provider for the united,' 'awakener of the people.' 'There is no doer of the action, and no experiencer of the result,' 'the undeceiver of the world,' 'clarity dependent on the four great elements.' In connection with `sarati` and `icchati`: 'he remembers his mother,' 'none remembers them,' 'for beings, due to kamma as condition,' 'he desires a son.' In connection with `karoti`: 'he counteracts the water,' 'he treats the wound,' the meaning is 'he prepares.' In the sense of the fifth case, even in connection with decline and fear, the sixth case occurs: 'they miss the Dhamma due to not hearing it,' 'why indeed should I fear that happiness?' 'All tremble at punishment,' 'all fear death,' 'afraid of the four deadly serpents, the terrible poisons,' and so on.

40. Tulyatthena vā tatiyā

40. With words meaning 'similar', alternatively the third case.

Tulyatthena yoge vā chaṭṭhī hoti tatiyā ca. Pitu tulyo, pitarā vā, mātu tulyo, mātarā vā.

In conjunction with a word meaning 'similar', the sixth case or the third case occurs. 'Similar to the father' (genitive), or 'similar to the father' (instrumental); 'similar to the mother' (genitive), or 'similar to the mother' (instrumental).

32. Sattamyā+dhāre

32. The seventh case in the sense of location.

Kattukammaṭṭhānaṃ nisajja+pacanādikriyānaṃ yo ādhāro, taṃ ādhārakārakaṃ nāma. Kathaṃ kaṭe nisīdati devadatto, thāliyaṃ odanaṃ pacati, devadatta+taṇḍulānaṃ kattu+kammānaṃ dhāraṇato tadaṭṭhaāsana+pacanakriyaṃ kaṭa+thāliyo dhārenti nāma, tasmiṃ sattamīvibhatti hoti.

That which is the support of actions such as sitting and cooking, which pertain to an agent and an object, is called the locative case. For example: Devadatta sits on a mat; he cooks rice in a pot. Because they support the agent, Devadatta, and the object, the rice, the mat and the pot are said to support the actions of sitting and cooking performed for their sake. In this sense, the seventh case-ending occurs.

So byāpiko, opasilesiko, vesayiko, sāmīpikoti catubbidho. Tattha yo ādheyyassa nissesādhārabhūto, so byāpiko, yathā tilesu telaṃ atthi, khīresu jalaṃ, dadhimhi sappi. Paccekasiddhānaṃ bhāvānaṃ yaṃ ādheyyabhāvena upasilesanaṃ allīyanaṃ atthi, so opasilesiko. Yathā āsane nisinno saṅgho, thāliyaṃ odanaṃ pacati, ghaṭe udaka+matthi, dūre ṭhito, samīpe ṭhito. Yattha samīpe samīpīvohāraṃ katvā tadāyattatādīpanatthaṃ ādhārabhāvo upacarīyati, taṃ sāmīpikaṃ, yathā gaṅgāyaṃ ghoso, gaṅgāya samīpe vajotyattho. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane. Yattha aññathābhāvavasena desantarāvacchedavasena vā ādhāraparikappo[M 0.0128], so vesayito. Yathā ākāse sakuṇā caranti, bhūmiyaṃ manussā, jale macchā, pāsādesu patito, pāpasmiṃ ramatī mano, pasanno buddhasāsane, paññāya sādhu, vinaye nipuṇo, mātari sādhu, pitari nipuṇo.

It is fourfold: pervasive, contiguous, locative of scope, and proximate. Herein, that which is the complete support of the supported is pervasive, as in 'there is oil in sesame seeds,' 'water in milk,' 'ghee in curds.' That which has the nature of adhering or clinging to individually established things as the supported is contiguous. For example: 'the Sangha seated on a seat,' 'he cooks rice in a pot,' 'there is water in a vessel,' 'standing far away,' 'standing nearby.' Where, by making use of the expression of proximity, the supporting nature is figuratively applied for the purpose of indicating dependence and so forth, that is proximate, as in 'a hamlet on the Ganges,' meaning 'near the Ganges.' 'He dwells at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove.' Where the supporting relation is conceived by way of difference in nature or by delimitation of region, that is locative of scope. For example: 'birds move in the sky,' 'humans on the ground,' 'fish in water,' 'fallen in the palaces,' 'the mind delights in evil,' 'one is confident in the Buddha's teaching,' 'good in wisdom,' 'expert in discipline,' 'good to his mother,' 'expert in regard to his father.'

Kiriyā kattu+kammaṭṭhā, ādhārīyati yena so;

Ādhāro catudhā vutto, byāpakādippabhedato.

Action, which pertains to an agent and an object, / is supported by that which is the support; / That support is said to be fourfold, / distinguished as pervasive and so forth.

Byāpako tilakhīrādi, kaṭo opasilesiko;

Sāmīpiko tu gaṅgādi, ākāso visayo mato.

Pervasive is as in sesame, milk, etc.; / Contiguous is as in a mat; / Proximate is as in the Ganges, etc.; / Space is considered the locative of scope.

33. Nimitte

33. In the Sense of Cause or Reason.

Nimittatthe sattamī hoti. Ajinamhi haññate dīpi, kuñjaro dantesu haññate, aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī, sampajānamusāvāde pācittiyaṃ. Sabbattha nimityattho.

The seventh case occurs in the sense of cause or reason. For example: "A leopard is killed for its skin"; "an elephant is killed for its tusks"; "one who sees danger in even minor faults"; "for a deliberate lie, there is a pācittiya offense." Everywhere, the sense is that of a cause or reason.

34. Yabbhāvo bhāvalakkhaṇaṃ

34. When the State of One is the Characteristic of Another.

Yassa bhāvo bhāvantarassa lakkhaṇaṃ bhavati, tato sattamī. Kāle gāvīsu duyhamānāsugato, duddhāsu āgato. Etthagamanakriyāya dohanakriyācihanaṃ, āgamanakriyāya duddhākriyācihanaṃ, eva+muparipi. Pubbaṇhasamaye gato, sāyanhasamaye āgato, jāyamāne kho sāriputta bodhisatte ayaṃ dasasahassī lokadhātu sampakampi.

When the state of one thing becomes the characteristic of another state, then the seventh case occurs. For example: "He went when the cows were being milked," "he came when they had been milked." Here, the act of milking is a mark for the act of going, and the act of having been milked is a mark for the act of coming; and so on further. "He went in the morning," "he came in the evening." "When the Bodhisatta was being born, O Sāriputta, this ten-thousandfold world-system shook."

Pāsāṇā sakkharā ceva, kaṭhalā khāṇukaṇṭakā;

Sabbe maggā vivajjanti, gacchante lokanāyake.

Stones and pebbles, / gravel, stumps, and thorns— / all clear away from the path / as the Leader of the World proceeds.

Imasmiṃ [M 0.0129] sati idaṃ hoti iccādi. “Akāle vassatī tassa, kāle tassa na vassatī”ti visayasattamī.

When this exists, that comes to be, and so forth. "It rains for him out of season, and it does not rain for him in season" is a locative of scope.

35. Chaṭṭhī cā+nādare

35. The Sixth Case, and in the Sense of Disregard.

Yassa bhāvo bhāvantarassa lakkhaṇaṃ bhavati, tato chaṭṭhī hoti sattamī cā+nādare gamyamāne. Akāmakānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ rudantānaṃ pabbaji, mātāpitūsu rudantesu vā. “Ākoṭayanto so neti, sivirājassa pekkhate”, “maccu ādāya gacchati, pekkhamāne mahājane”.

When the state of one thing becomes the characteristic of another state, then the sixth case or the seventh case occurs when disregard is implied. For example: "He went forth while his unwilling parents were weeping," or "while his parents were weeping." "Striking, he leads him away, while the Sivi king watches." "Death takes him away, while the great crowd watches."

Gunnaṃ sāmīti sambandhe chaṭṭhī, gosu sāmīti visayasattamī. Evaṃ gunnamissaro, gosvi+ssaro, gunnaṃ adhipati, gosu adhipati, gunnaṃ dāyādo, gosu dāyādo, gunnaṃ sakkhī, gosu sakkhī, gunnaṃ patibhū, gosu patibhū, gunnaṃ pasuto, gosu pasuto, kusalā naccagītassa, kusalā naccagīte, āyutto kaṭakaraṇassa, āyutto kaṭakaraṇe. Tathā ādhāravacanicchāyaṃ sattamī, bhikkhūsu abhivādenti, muddhani cumbitvā, bāhāsu gahetvā, hatthesu piṇḍāya caranti, kadalīsu gaje rakkhanti, ñāṇasmiṃ pasanno, ñāṇasmiṃ ussukkoti visayasattamī.

The sixth case is used in the sense of connection, as in "lord of cows" (gunnaṃ sāmī); the seventh case is used in the sense of locative of scope, as in "lord among cows" (gosu sāmī). Similarly: "master of cows" (gunnaṃ issaro), "master among cows" (gosu issaro); "ruler of cows" (gunnaṃ adhipati), "ruler among cows" (gosu adhipati); "heir of cows" (gunnaṃ dāyādo), "heir among cows" (gosu dāyādo); "witness of cows" (gunnaṃ sakkhī), "witness among cows" (gosu sakkhī); "guarantor of cows" (gunnaṃ patibhū), "guarantor among cows" (gosu patibhū); "devoted to cows" (gunnaṃ pasuto), "devoted among cows" (gosu pasuto); "skilled in dancing and singing" (kusalā naccagītassa), "skilled in dancing and singing" (kusalā naccagīte); "engaged in handicrafts" (āyutto kaṭakaraṇassa), "engaged in handicrafts" (āyutto kaṭakaraṇe). Likewise, the seventh case is used when the sense of support is intended: "they pay respect to the monks" (bhikkhūsu abhivādenti), "having kissed on the head" (muddhani cumbitvā), "having taken by the arms" (bāhāsu gahetvā), "they go for alms with bowls in their hands" (hatthesu piṇḍāya caranti), "they protect elephants among the banana trees" (kadalīsu gaje rakkhanti), "confident in knowledge" (ñāṇasmiṃ pasanno), "zealous in knowledge" (ñāṇasmiṃ ussukko) — these are locatives of scope.

36. Yato niddhāraṇaṃ

36. From Which There is Determination.

Jātiguṇakriyāhi samudāyate+kadesassa puthakkaraṇaṃ niddhāraṇaṃ, yato taṃ karīyati, tato chaṭṭhīsattamiyo honti. Sālayo sūkadhaññānaṃ pathyatamā, sūkadhaññesu sālayo pathyatamā. Kaṇhā gāvīnaṃ sampannakhīratamā, kaṇhā gāvīsu [M 0.0130] sampannakhīratamā. Gacchataṃ dhāvanto sīghatamā, gacchantesu dhāvanto sīghatamā.

Determination is the separation of a part from a whole by means of genus, quality, or action. From that from which it is done, the sixth and seventh cases occur. For example: "Among coarse grains, rice is the most wholesome," or "among coarse grains, rice is the most wholesome." "Among cows, the black one is the most abundant in milk," or "among cows, the black one is the most abundant in milk." "Among those walking, the runner is the fastest," or "among those walking, the runner is the fastest."

14. Sattamyā+dhikye

14. The Seventh in the Sense of Excess.

Ādhikye atthe upena yuttamhā sattamī hoti. Upakhāriyaṃ doṇo, khāriyā doṇo adhikotyattho. Tathā upanikkhe kahāpaṇaṃ.

The seventh case occurs when conjoined with 'upa' in the sense of excess. 'Upakhāriyaṃ doṇo' means 'a doṇa is more than a khāri'. Similarly, 'upanikkhe kahāpaṇaṃ'.

15. Sāmitthe+dhinā

15. With 'Adhi' in the Sense of Ownership.

Sāmibhāvatthe adhinā yuttamhā sattamī hoti. Adhibrahmadatte pañcālā, adhipañcālesu brahmadatto, brahmadattissarā pañcālāti attho. Adhidevesu buddho, sammutidevādīhi buddho adhikotyattho.

The seventh case occurs when conjoined with 'adhi' in the sense of ownership. 'Adhibrahmadatte pañcālā' (the Pañcālas are under Brahmadatta), 'adhipañcālesu brahmadatto' (Brahmadatta is over the Pañcālas); the meaning is that the Pañcālas are under the authority of Brahmadatta. 'Adhidevesu buddho' (the Buddha is over the gods) means the Buddha is superior to conventional gods and others.

Ettha ca yathāvuttesu atthesu ayaṃ bhedo –

And here, in these meanings as stated, this is the distinction:

Kārakaṃ sādhakaṃ nibbattakaṃ kriyānimittanti atthato ekameva, tañca daṇḍo, dhavalo, pacanaṃ, citto, goti dabba+guṇa+kriyā+nāma+jātibhedena pañcavidhampi kamma+kattādivasena chabbidhaṃ, taṃ sattikārakaṃ, tadādhārabhūtadabbādayo tatraṭṭhakārakaṃ, na mukhyato. Mukhyato ce honti, tesaṃ sattidabbānaṃ aññamaññabyāvaṭarūpattā yo ādhāro, so ādhāroyeva, kismiñcikāle karaṇaṃ vā katturūpabhūto vā na hoti, tasmā thāli pacati, thāliyā pacati, thāliyaṃ pacatītyādinā ekassa vatthuno kattu+karaṇā+dhārabhedo na siyā. Sattipakkhe pana dabbādīnaṃ anekasattiyā ādhārattā sattiyā dabbādayo vivakkhitā taṃ taṃ kārakaṃ hotīti dabbādīnaṃ abhedepi kārakabhedo yujjate. Vuttañhi –

The kāraka, the accomplisher, the producer, the cause of action—these are one in meaning. And that kāraka, though fivefold by the distinctions of substance (e.g., a stick), quality (e.g., white), action (e.g., cooking), name (e.g., Citta), and species (e.g., a cow), is also sixfold by way of object, agent, etc. That is the power-kāraka. The substances and so forth which are its basis are the kāraka residing therein, not the primary kāraka. If they were primary, then since the power and the substance have mutually distinct forms, whatever is the support would be only the support; at no time would it be the instrument or take the form of the agent. Therefore, for one and the same thing, there would be no distinction of agent, instrument, and support, as in 'the pot cooks,' 'one cooks by the pot,' 'one cooks in the pot.' But on the side of the power-theory, since substances and so forth are the support of many powers, the substances and so forth, when intended through a particular power, become that particular kāraka. Thus, even when there is no distinction in the substances themselves, a distinction of kāraka is justified. For it is said—

Vicittakattuādīhi[M 0.0131], saṃyogā ekavatthuno;

Nānāttaṃ yujjate nāṭya-bhedena naṭakassi+vāti.

For a single thing, through connection with various agents and so forth, / diversity is justified, like that of an actor through different roles.

Thāli vatthuto ekā cedapi sattikārakabhūtakattu+karaṇā+dhārādīnaṃ bhedena bheda+mupayāti, kimiva rāma+rāvaṇādivesadhārīnaṭako tesaṃ nāmavasena rāmo, rāvaṇoti bheda+mupayāti, ta+mivāti adhippāyo.

Even though the pot is one in reality, it undergoes division by the distinctions of agent, instrument, support, etc., which are in the nature of power-kārakas. Just as an actor wearing the guise of Rāma, Rāvaṇa, etc., undergoes distinction as Rāma or Rāvaṇa by virtue of their names—this is the intended meaning.

Puna+rapi –

And again—

Yathe+kopi paṭo sutta, pītādiguṇasaṃyuto;

Sukko paṭoti pītoti, bhedaṃ yātye+vameva+yaṃ.

Just as a single cloth, composed of thread and endowed with qualities such as yellow, undergoes distinction as 'a white cloth' or 'a yellow cloth'; even so does this kāraka.

Ettha ca sattibhūtakattādayo mukhyakārakaṃ, taṃyogena dabbabhūtathālī guṇakārakaṃ, te ca kathaṃ kriyāya kārakā honti. Kattā attanā patiṭṭhitāya hasati+naccaticcādikriyāya nimittaṃ hoti. Kammañca attanā patiṭṭhitakriyāya tadatthabhūtaindhanādīni pavattentaṃ “odanaṃ pacatī”tyādo nimittaṃ. ‘Kaṭṭhehi paccatī’tyādo kaṭṭhāni jalanakriyāya sādhetabbapākassa aṅgabhāvena nimittaṃ. ‘Pharasunā chindatī’tyādo pharasu ca kaṭṭhānaṃ dvidhāpavattiyā nimittaṃ. Kammañca kriyāya sambandhīyamānabyāpye sati nimittabhāvena kriyāya nimittaṃ. Tathā sampadānā+vadhi+ādhārānaṃ ‘gāvo dadāti’ ‘gāmasmā apanayati’ ‘thāliyaṃ pacatī’tyādīsu godānā+panayana+pacanakriyānaṃ nimittattā kriyāya nimittāni honti. Tesaṃ yathāsakaṃ kriyāya pavattako kattā, tasmā sa eva padhāno kattāti vohāraṃ [M 0.0132] labhati, aññesaṃ karaṇādīnaṃ kattubhāve satipi appadhānattā taṃ na labhati.

Here, the agent and other such kārakas, which are in the nature of a power, are the primary kārakas. Through connection with them, the pot, being a substance, becomes a secondary kāraka. And how are they kārakas of the action? The agent becomes the condition for actions such as laughing and dancing, which are established by himself. And the object, by causing things such as fuel, which serve the purpose of the action established by itself, to proceed, becomes the condition, as in 'cooks rice'. In 'cooks with firewood', the firewood becomes the condition as an ancillary part of the cooking to be achieved by the action of burning. In 'cuts with an axe', the axe is the condition for the wood's splitting into two. The object, when it is that which is to be pervaded by being connected to the action, becomes the condition for the action by being a cause. Similarly, in cases such as 'gives cows', 'takes away from the village', or 'cooks in a pot', the recipient, the point of departure, and the location become conditions for the action by being conditions for the actions of giving cows, taking away, and cooking, respectively. Of these, the agent is the impeller of the action according to its own function; therefore, he alone gains the designation of principal agent. Although the others, such as the instrument, possess agency, they do not gain this designation due to their subordinate role.

Codakena vuttañhi –

For it was said by the objector—

Nanu sāmagyamīnāyaṃ, kriyāsiddhi kathaṃ vada;

Ekassa kattuno eva, sabbesaṃ kattutaṃ vinā.

Surely this harmony is to be affirmed? Tell me, how can there be accomplishment of an action when there is only one agent, without the agency of all others?

Sabbesaṃ karaṇādīnaṃ, kattutāya viyogato;

Karaṇādīnaṃ abhāvattā, kārakaṃ na hi chabbidhanti.

Due to the dissociation from the agency of all instruments and so forth, and due to the absence of instruments and so forth, the kāraka is surely not sixfold.

Vuccate –

It is said in reply—

Yadyapya+tthi hi kattuttaṃ, sabhāvā karaṇādisu;

Kriyāsiddhyā tathāpye+ta+mappadhānaṃ paraṅgato.

Although there is indeed agency by nature in instruments and so forth, yet for the accomplishment of the action, this agency is subordinate, as it serves another.

Etaṃ sabhāvato upalabbhamānaṃ karaṇādīsu kattuttaṃ paresaṃ karaṇādīnaṃ jalana+dhāraṇādikriyāya aṅgaṃ upāyati appadhānanti adhippāyo.

The meaning is that this agency, which is found to exist by nature in instruments and so forth, becomes an ancillary part to the actions of burning, holding, and so forth, of other instruments and so forth; thus, it is subordinate.

Kārakaṃ chabbidhaṃ saññā-vasā chabbīsatividhaṃ;

Pabhedā sattadhā kammaṃ, kattā pañcavidho bhave.

The kāraka is sixfold; by way of designation, it is twenty-sixfold. The object has seven divisions; the agent may be fivefold.

Karaṇaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti, sampadānaṃ tidhā mataṃ;

Apādānaṃ pañcavidhaṃ, ādhāro tu catubbidho.

The instrument is twofold, the recipient is considered threefold, the point of departure is fivefold, and the location is fourfold.

Vibhattiyo pana –

As for the case meanings—

Paccatta+mupayogañca, karaṇaṃ sampadāniyaṃ;

Nissakkaṃ sāmivacanaṃ, bhumma+mālapana+ṭṭhamaṃti.

The agent, the object, the instrument, the recipient, the point of departure, the possessor, the location, and the vocative as the eighth.

Iti payogasiddhiyaṃ kārakakaṇḍo tatiyo.

Thus ends the third chapter, the chapter on kārakas, in the Payogasiddhi.

4. Samāsakaṇḍa

4. The Chapter on Compounds

Atha [M 0.0133] nāmānameva aññamaññasambandhīnaṃ samāsoti nāmanissitattā, sayañca nāmikattā nāmānantaraṃ samāso vuccate.

Then, a compound is a combination of mutually related nouns; and because it is dependent on nouns and is itself nominal, the compound is discussed immediately after nouns.

1. Syādi syādine+katthanti

1. A Word with a Case Ending with a Word with a Case Ending into a Single Meaning

Ida+madhikataṃ veditabbaṃ. Pubbe vuttavidhiggahaṇañāyena syādīti tadantassa gahaṇaṃ. So ca bhinnatthānaṃ nāmāna+mekatthībhāvo samāsoti vuccate.

This should be understood as the governing rule. By the principle of grasping what is stated in a rule, 'syādi' refers to that which ends in a 'syādi' suffix. And that unification into a single meaning of nouns with distinct meanings is called a compound.

2. Asaṅkhyaṃ vibhatti+sampatti+samīpa+sākalyā+bhāva+yathā+ pacchā+yugapadatthe

2. The Indeclinable Compound (Asaṅkhya) is formed in the meanings of case, prosperity, proximity, totality, absence, 'according to', 'after', and simultaneity.

Pubbassa+tthaparaṃ yassa, aññatthaparamañca yaṃ;

Napuṃsakaṃ bhave yañca, ta+dāsaṃkhya+mihe+ssate.

That in which the meaning of the prior term is principal, that in which the meaning of another term is principal, and that which is neuter—that is here considered an indeclinable compound (asaṅkhya).

Satthantare pasiddhaṃ yaṃ, abyayībhāvanāmato;

Upakumbhaṃ tiṭṭhagu ca, pātameghaṃti taṃ yathā.

That which is well-known in other grammatical treatises by the name of 'abyayībhāva', such as upakumbhaṃ, tiṭṭhagu, and pātameghaṃ.

Asaṅkhyaṃ syādyantaṃ vibhatyādīna+matthe vattamānaṃ syādyantena sahe+katthaṃ bhavati. “Aviggaho niccasamāso, padantaraviggaho ce”ti padantaraviggaho. Itthīsu tathā pavattāti viggayha vibhatyatthe samāse kate –

An indeclinable compound (asaṅkhya), ending in a case suffix and existing in the meanings of case and so forth, becomes one meaning with another word ending in a case suffix. 'A permanent compound is without an analytical phrase; and if there is an analytical phrase, it is with other words'—thus it is an analysis with other words. Having analyzed 'it occurs thus in regard to women,' when the compound is formed in the meaning of the case ending—

2,119. Ekatthatāyaṃ

2,119. When there is a Single Meaning

Eko attho yassa pakatipaccayādisamudāyassa so ekattho. Tassa bhāvo pavattinimittaṃ ekatthatā, īyādi+ṇādi+samāsavidhānaṃ, tasmiṃ sati syādilopo hoti.

That collection of base, suffix, and so forth which has one meaning is 'that which has one meaning' (ekattho). The state of that, the condition for its occurrence, is 'singleness of meaning' (ekatthatā). When there is this, which is the rule for taddhita suffixes like īya, primary suffixes like ṇa, and compounding, there is elision of case suffixes.

9. Taṃ napuṃsakanti

9. That is Neuter

Napuṃsakaliṅge [M 0.0134] ca “pubbasmā+mādito”ti sabbavibhattīnaṃ lope ca kate adhitthi tiṭṭhati, bho adhitthi, adhitthi passa, adhitthi kataṃ, adhitti carati, adhitthi dehi, adhitthi apehi, adhitthi āyattaṃ, adhitthi patiṭṭhitaṃ. Evaṃ adhikumāri, antabhūtassa appadhānassa ghapassa “ghapassa+ntassā+ppadhānassā”ti passa rasso.

And in the neuter gender, when the elision of all case suffixes is made according to the rule 'from the prior member of a compound, from the beginning...', the forms are: adhitthi tiṭṭhati, bho adhitthi, adhitthi passa, adhitthi kataṃ, adhitthi carati, adhitthi dehi, adhitthi apehi, adhitthi āyattaṃ, adhitthi patiṭṭhitaṃ. Similarly, in adhikumāri, the final vowel of the subordinate 'ghapa' stem is shortened according to the rule 'of a final, subordinate ghapa stem...'

Saha=sampannaṃ brahmaṃ sabrahmaṃ. Vuttanayena ettha ca upari ca samāsādayo honti, ettha “akāle satatthe”ti sahassa sādeso. Syādimhi kate “pubbasmā+mādito”ti syādīnaṃ lope ca sampatte “nā+to+mapañcamiyā”ti apañcamiyā paṭisedho ca akārantaasaṃkhyasamāsato parāsaṃ sabbavibhattīnaṃ aṃādeso ca hoti. Eva+muparipi.

Brahma endowed with 'saha' is sabrahmaṃ. According to the stated method, compounds and so forth are formed here and further on; here, by the rule 'in the meaning of 'sat', not in the meaning of 'kāla'', there is the substitution of 'sā' for 'saha'. When a case suffix is applied, and when the elision of case suffixes is about to occur according to the rule 'from the prior member of a compound, from the beginning...', the prohibition for non-ablative cases occurs by the rule 'not after 'a' except for the fifth case', and the substitution of 'aṃ' for all case suffixes following an a-ending indeclinable compound (asaṅkhya) also occurs. Similarly in the following cases.

Bhikkhānaṃ samiddhi subhikkhaṃ, ettha ghassa rasso. Subhikkhaṃ tiṭṭhati bho subhikkhaṃ, subhikkhaṃ passa. Nā+smiṃsu “vā tatiyā sattamīnaṃ”ti vikappena aṃ, subhikkhaṃ subhikkhena vā kataṃ, subhikkhaṃ subhikkhena vā carati, subhikkhaṃ dehi. Pañcamiyaṃ a+mabbhāvā subhikkhā apagaccha, subhikkha+māyattaṃ, subhikkhaṃ subhikkhe vā patiṭṭhitaṃ.

The prosperity of alms-food is subhikkhaṃ; here, the 'gha' stem is shortened. Examples: Subhikkhaṃ tiṭṭhati, bho subhikkhaṃ, subhikkhaṃ passa. By the rule 'optionally for the third and seventh cases', the substitution of 'aṃ' is optional, for example: subhikkhaṃ or subhikkhena vā kataṃ; subhikkhaṃ or subhikkhena vā carati; subhikkhaṃ dehi. In the fifth case, as there is no substitution of 'aṃ', the form is: subhikkhā apagaccha. Other examples: subhikkhaṃ āyattaṃ; subhikkhaṃ or subhikkhe vā patiṭṭhitaṃ.

Samīpatthe-kumbhassa samīpaṃ upakumbhaṃ, evaṃ upanagaraṃ, bho upakumbhaṃ iccādi.

In the meaning of proximity: 'Near the pot' is upakumbhaṃ; similarly, upanagaraṃ; 'O upakumbhaṃ', and so forth.

Sākalye-tiṇampi asesetvāti satiṇaṃ, tiṇampi asesetvā ajjhoharaṇīya+majjhoharatītyattho. Sesaṃ sabrahmasamaṃ[M 0.0135]. Aggimpi asesetvāti sāggi, aggiganthaṃpi asesetvā adhītetyattho. Vāraggahaṇaṃ adhitthisamaṃ.

In the meaning of totality: 'Including even the grass' is satiṇaṃ; the meaning is 'one consumes what is to be consumed, including even the grass, leaving nothing.' The rest is similar to sabrahmaṃ. 'Including even the fire' is sāggi; the meaning is 'one studies, including even the fire-text, leaving nothing.' The declension of the i-stem is similar to adhitthi.

Abhāvo sambandhībhedā bahuvidho, tatra iddhābhāvevigatā iddhi=vibhūti saddikānanti dussaddikaṃ. Atthābhāvemakkhikānaṃ abhāvo nimmakkhikaṃ, niddarathaṃ, nimmasakaṃ. Atikkamābhāve-atigatāni tiṇāni nittiṇaṃ. Upabhogasambandhīvattamānakālassa abhāve-atigataṃ lahupāvuraṇaṃ atilahupāvuraṇaṃ, lahupāvuraṇassa nā+yaṃ upabhogatā loti attho.

Absence is of many kinds due to differences in what is related. There, in the absence of psychic power: 'psychic power, or splendor, of those with sound, is gone' is dussaddikaṃ. In the absence of things: 'absence of flies' is nimmakkhikaṃ; similarly, niddarathaṃ, nimmasakaṃ. In the sense of going beyond: 'grasses are gone beyond' is nittiṇaṃ. In the absence of the present time related to enjoyment: 'a light covering is gone beyond' is atilahupāvuraṇaṃ; the meaning is 'this is not the time for enjoying a light covering'.

Yathāttho+nekavidho, tatra yoggatāyaṃ-yoggaṃ rūpa+manurūpaṃ. Vicchāyaṃ-addhamāsaṃ addhamāsaṃ anu anvaddhamāsaṃ, evaṃ paccattaṃ. Atthānativattiyaṃ-sattiṃ anatikkamma yathāsatti. Evaṃ yathākkamaṃ, yathābalaṃ. Bahulādhikārā yā yā parisā yathāparisā. Sadisatthe-kikhiyā kaṇhavicchitadhenuyā sadiso sakikhi, sahassa sādeso. Ānupubbiyaṃ-jeṭṭhānukkamena anujeṭṭhaṃ.

The meaning of 'yathā' is of many kinds. There, in suitability: 'suitable form' is anurūpaṃ. In repetition: 'following half-month by half-month' is anvaddhamāsaṃ; similarly, paccattaṃ. In not transgressing the meaning: 'without transgressing one's capacity' is yathāsatti. Similarly, yathākkamaṃ, yathābalaṃ. By the governing rule of 'bahula': 'whatever assembly' is yathāparisā. In the meaning of similarity: 'similar to a speckled cow named Kikhi' is sakikhi; there is the substitution of 'sā' for 'saha'. In sequence: 'in the order of elders' is anujeṭṭhaṃ.

Pacchāatthe-rathassa pacchā anurathaṃ.

In the sense of 'after': 'behind the chariot' is anurathaṃ.

Yugapadatthe-cakkena saha=ekakālaṃ sacakkaṃ, cakkena ekakkhaṇe nidhetīti attho.

In the sense of simultaneity: 'with the wheel at the same time' is sacakkaṃ; the meaning is, 'one places it at the same moment as the wheel'.

3. Yathā na tulye

3. With yathā, not in the sense of 'comparable'.

Yathāsaddo tulyatthe vattamāno syādyantena sahe+kattho na bhavati. Yathā devadatto, tathā yaññadatto. Ettha upamānabhūto yathāsaddo ‘tathā yaññadatto’ti upameyya+mapekkhati, tasmā “sāpekkha+masamatthaṃ bhavatī”ti ñāyā asamāse [M 0.0136] “na tulye”ti paṭisedho kimattha+miti ce. Yasmā “yathā devadatto”ti samudāyameva upamānaṃ bhavati, na visuṃ yathāsaddo, tasmā samudāyasseva upameyyasāpekkhatte na asāmatthiyatā na visuṃ yathāsaddassa, tasmā sādisse pattasamāsassa paṭisedhattha+midaṃ. Tulyattheti vattabbe tulyaṃ vinā tulyatā natthīti tulyattheti avatvā tulyeti vuttaṃ.

The word yathā, when occurring in the sense of similarity, does not form a single meaning with a word ending in a case suffix. For example: 'As Devadatta, so Yaññadatta.' Here, the word yathā, serving as the standard of comparison, requires an object of comparison, namely 'so Yaññadatta.' Therefore, if by the maxim 'what is dependent is incapable of compounding,' there is no compounding, what is the purpose of the prohibition 'not in the sense of "comparable"'? Because in 'as Devadatta,' the entire phrase becomes the standard of comparison, not the word yathā separately. Therefore, since it is the entire phrase that is dependent on the object of comparison, there is no incapability of compounding for the word yathā separately. Hence, this rule is for the purpose of prohibiting a compound that would otherwise be possible in the sense of similarity. Although tulyatthe ('in the sense of similarity') should have been stated, since there is no similarity without something that is similar, instead of saying tulyatthe, tulye ('in the sense of "comparable"') is stated.

Yathākathañci sādissaṃ, ñāyate yattha sambhavaṃ;

Upamā nāma sā tassā, papañco bahudhā bhave.

In whatever way a similarity is known, wherever it may arise; that is called a simile, and its elaboration is manifold.

4. Yāvā+vadhāraṇe

4. With yāva, in the sense of limitation.

Yāvasaddo avadhāraṇe vattamāno syādyantena sahe+kattho bhavati. Avadhāraṇaṃ=ettakatāparicchedo. Yāvantāni amattāni=bhājanāni yāvāmattaṃ, iminā samāse kate sesaṃ pubbasamaṃ. Jīvassa yattako paricchedo yāvajīvaṃ. Yāvatāyukaṃ, “sakatthe”ti kapaccayo. Yattakena attho yāvadatthaṃ.

The word yāva, when occurring in the sense of limitation, forms a single meaning with a word ending in a case suffix. Limitation means the determination of a certain quantity. 'As many vessels as there are' (yāvantāni amattāni) becomes yāvāmattaṃ. When a compound is formed by this rule, the remaining operations are similar to the preceding examples. The extent of a being's life is yāvajīvaṃ. In yāvatāyukaṃ, the suffix ka is in the sense of 'its own meaning'. That which has a certain purpose is yāvadatthaṃ.

5. Payyapā bahi tiro pure pacchā vā pañcamyā

5. The particles pari, apa, ā, bahi, tiro, pure, and pacchā are compounded optionally with a word ending in the fifth case.

Pariādayo pañcamyantena sahe+katthā honti vā. Pari pabbatā paripabbataṃ. Vāssa vākyavikappatthattā pari pabbatā iccādayopi honti. Apa pabbatā apapabbataṃ, ā pāṭaliputtā āpāṭaliputtaṃ, bahi gāmā bahigāmaṃ, tiro pabbatā tiropabbataṃ, pure bhattā purebhattaṃ, pacchā bhattā pacchābhattaṃ, sabbaṃ upakumbhasamaṃ, iminā samāso viseso. Eva+muparisuttepi.

Pari and so on optionally form a single meaning with a word ending in the fifth case. For example, pari pabbatā becomes paripabbataṃ. Because vā (optionally) has the sense of an alternative phrasing, expressions such as pari pabbatā also occur. Apa pabbatā becomes apapabbataṃ; ā pāṭaliputtā becomes āpāṭaliputtaṃ; bahi gāmā becomes bahigāmaṃ; tiro pabbatā becomes tiropabbataṃ; pure bhattā becomes purebhattaṃ; pacchā bhattā becomes pacchābhattaṃ. All are similar to upakumbha. The compound formed by this rule is a special case. This is also the case in the preceding rule.

Vātya+dhikāro [M 0.0137] –

The governing rule of vā (optionally) begins.

6. Samīpā+yāmesva+nu

6. With anu, in the senses of proximity and extent.

“Asaṃkhya”miccādinā niccasamāsassa vikappatthaṃ samīpaggahaṇaṃ. Anusaddo sāmīpye āyāme ca vattamāno syādyantena sahe+kattho vā hoti. Ettha samīpaggahaṇassa bhāvappadhānattā sāmīpyameva gamyateti sāmīpyeti vuttaṃ. Vanassa anu=samīpaṃ anuvanaṃ, gaṅgāya anu=āyāmo anugaṅgaṃ, gaṅgāya anu vā bārāṇasī.

The inclusion of samīpa (proximity) is for making optional the obligatory compound prescribed by the rule beginning with Asaṃkhya. The word anu, when occurring in the senses of proximity and extent, optionally forms a single meaning with a word ending in a case suffix. Here, because the inclusion of samīpa has the primary sense of the abstract noun, proximity (sāmīpya) is understood; hence sāmīpye is stated. Anu vanassa (near the forest) becomes anuvanaṃ. Anu gaṅgāya (along the length of the Ganges) becomes anugaṅgaṃ. Or, as an uncompounded phrase: gaṅgāya anu bārāṇasī (Bārāṇasī is along the Ganges).

7. Tiṭṭhagvādīni

7. Tiṭṭhagu and so on.

Tiṭṭhaguādīni aññatthena siddhāpi asmiṃ asaṃkhyasamāse nipātiyanti. Tiṭṭhanti gāvo yasmiṃ kāleti tiṭṭhantasadda+gosaddehi paṭhamāyomhi kate “vā+nekaññatthe”ti samāso, iminā nipātanā lope napuṃsakatthe ca kate simhi gossa “gossu”ti ukāre “pubbasmā+mādito”ti vibhattilopo. Evaṃ vahantī gāvo yasmiṃ kāleti vahaggu iccādi. Velāppakāsakapātoādīnampi ettheva saṅgaho, pāto nahānanti sattamīamādisamāse pātanahānaṃ, evaṃ sāyanahānaṃ, pātakālaṃ, sāyakālaṃ, pātameghaṃ, sāyameghaṃ, pātamaggaṃ, sāyamaggaṃ, ettha “eona+ma vaṇṇe”ti akāro, niggahītassa lopo ca hoti.

The forms Tiṭṭhagu and so on, though established in another sense, are irregularly formed in this asaṃkhyasamāsa. The phrase tiṭṭhanti gāvo yasmiṃ kāle ('the time in which cows stand') is formed from the words tiṭṭhanta and go with the first case endings, the compound being formed by the rule vānekaññatthe. By this irregular formation, after the elision of the final of the first member and the assignment of the neuter gender, when the nominative singular ending si follows, the vowel u is substituted for go by the rule gossu, and the case ending is elided by pubbasmāmādito. Similarly, vahanti gāvo yasmiṃ kāle ('the time in which cows are yoked') becomes vahaggu, and so on. Words indicating time, such as pāto (morning), are also included here. For example, pāto nahānaṃ ('bathing in the morning') becomes pātanahānaṃ in a seventh-case amādi compound. Likewise, sāyanahānaṃ (evening bath), pātakālaṃ (morning time), sāyakālaṃ (evening time), pātameghaṃ (morning cloud), sāyameghaṃ (evening cloud), pātamaggaṃ (morning path), and sāyamaggaṃ (evening path). Here, by a rule such as etonam a vaṇṇe, there is the substitution of the vowel a and the elision of the niggahīta.

8. Ore+pari+paṭi+pāre+majjhe+heṭṭhu+ddhā+dho+nto vā chaṭṭhiyā.

8. The particles ora, upari, paṭi, pāra, majjha, heṭṭhā, uddhaṃ, adho, and anto are compounded optionally with a word ending in the sixth case.

Orādayo saddā chaṭṭhiyantena sahe+katthā vā honti. Oraṃ gaṅgāya oregaṅgā, upari sikharassa uparisikharaṃ, paṭi=mukhaṃ sotassa [M 0.0138] paṭisotaṃ, pāraṃ yamunāya pāreyamunaṃ, majjhaṃ gaṅgāya majjhegaṅgaṃ, heṭṭhā pāsādassa heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ, uddhaṃ gaṅgāya uddhagaṅgaṃ, adho gaṅgāya adhogaṅgaṃ, anto pāsādassa antopāsādaṃ. Iminā nipātanāva niggahītalope ca ekāre ca kate oreccādi hoti.

The words ora and so on optionally form a single meaning with a word ending in the sixth case. For example, oraṃ gaṅgāya becomes oregaṅgaṃ (on this side of the Ganges); upari sikharassa becomes uparisikharaṃ (above the peak); paṭi sotassa (facing the stream) becomes paṭisotaṃ (against the stream); pāraṃ yamunāya becomes pāreyamunaṃ (beyond the Yamunā); majjhaṃ gaṅgāya becomes majjhegaṅgaṃ (in the middle of the Ganges); heṭṭhā pāsādassa becomes heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ (beneath the palace); uddhaṃ gaṅgāya becomes uddhagaṅgaṃ (above the Ganges); adho gaṅgāya becomes adhogaṅgaṃ (below the Ganges); anto pāsādassa becomes antopāsādaṃ (inside the palace). By this very irregular formation, with the elision of the niggahīta and the substitution of e, forms such as oregaṅgaṃ are produced.

10. A+mādi

10. The Amādi Compounds

A+mādisyādyantaṃ syādyantena saha bahula+mekattaṃ hoti.

A word ending in a case suffix, from the accusative onwards, is variously compounded into a single meaning with another word ending in a case suffix.

Uttarassa padassa+ttho, padhānaṃ liṅga+massa ca;

Dutiyantādipadekattho, bahudhā taṃ vibhajjate.

The meaning of the latter word is principal, as is its gender; this compound, formed with words beginning with one in the second case, is divided in many ways.

Paresa+missate tañca, bhiyyo tappurisā+khyayā;

Taṃ yathā+tra rājāpaccaṃ, katthacīti+mitīdisaṃ.

And it is mixed with others; it is mostly known by the name Tappurisa. For example, here rājāpaccaṃ, and in some places, compounds involving iti and the like.

A+mādyantānaṃ kārakānaṃ akārakānañca samāso katthacimeva vā hoti. Tañca bahulaṃvidhānenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The compounding of words ending in the accusative case and so on, whether they express a case relation (kāraka) or not, occurs only in some instances, and is optional. And this should be understood as being governed by the principle of 'various application' (bahula).

Tattha dutiyātappuriso amādi gata+nissitā+tītā+tikkanta+pattā+pannādīhi bhavati. Saraṇaṃ gatoti samāse kate “ekatthatāyaṃ”ti vibhattilopādi upari sabbattha pubbasamaṃ. Saraṇagato, saraṇagatā. Saraṇagatā, saraṇagatāyo. Saraṇagataṃ kulaṃ, saraṇagatāni kulāni iccādi. Araññagato, bhūmigato. Dhammaṃ nissito dhammanissito, atthanissito. Bhavaṃ atīto bhavātīto, kālātīto. Pamāṇaṃ atikkantaṃ pamāṇātikkantaṃ, lokātikkantaṃ. Sukhaṃ patto sukhappatto, dukkhappatto. Sotaṃ āpanno sotāpanno, nirodhasamāpanno, maggappaṭipanno. Rathaṃ āruḷho rathāruḷho[M 0.0139]. Sabbarattiṃ sobhaṇo sabbarattisobhaṇo, muhuttasukhaṃ. Akārakānaṃ samāso accantasaṃyoge. Vuttiyevo+papadasamāse, tassa niccattā. Yathā kammaṃ karotīti kammakāro, kumbhakāro, atthaṃ kāmetīti atthakāmo, dhammakāmo, dhammaṃ dhāretīti dhammadharo, vinayadharo. Sānaṃ pacatīti sapāko, tantaṃ vāyatīti tantavāyo, varaṃ āharatīti varāharo. Nta+māna+ktavantehi vākyameva. Dhammaṃ suṇanto, dhammaṃ suṇamāno, odanaṃ bhuttavā.

Therein, the Accusative Tappurisa compound is formed with a word in the accusative case and words such as gata (gone), nissita (dependent), atīta (passed beyond), atikkanta (surpassed), patta (attained), and āpanna (entered into). When a compound such as saraṇaṃ gato (gone to refuge) is formed, by the rule ekatthatāyaṃ, the elision of the case ending and other operations are everywhere similar to the preceding examples. For instance: saraṇagato, saraṇagatā (f.); saraṇagatā, saraṇagatāyo (f. pl.); saraṇagataṃ kulaṃ, saraṇagatāni kulāni. Also: araññagato (gone to the forest), bhūmigato (gone to the ground). Dhammaṃ nissito becomes dhammanissito (dependent on the Dhamma); atthanissito (dependent on the meaning). Bhavaṃ atīto becomes bhavātīto (passed beyond existence); kālātīto (passed beyond time). Pamāṇaṃ atikkantaṃ becomes pamāṇātikkantaṃ (surpassed measure); lokātikkantaṃ (surpassed the world). Sukhaṃ patto becomes sukhappatto (attained happiness); dukkhappatto (attained suffering). Sotaṃ āpanno becomes sotāpanno (stream-enterer); nirodhasamāpanno (attained cessation); maggappaṭipanno (entered upon the path). Rathaṃ āruḷho becomes rathāruḷho (mounted a chariot). The compounding of non-kāraka words occurs in the sense of continuous duration, for example: sabbarattiṃ sobhaṇo becomes sabbarattisobhaṇo (beautiful all night long); muhuttasukhaṃ (happiness for a moment). In usage, this is like an Upapada compound, due to its obligatory nature. For example: kammaṃ karotīti becomes kammakāro (worker); kumbhakāro (potter). Atthaṃ kāmetīti becomes atthakāmo (one who desires the meaning); dhammakāmo (one who desires the Dhamma). Dhammaṃ dhāretīti becomes dhammadharo (one who upholds the Dhamma); vinayadharo (one who upholds the Vinaya). Sānaṃ pacatīti becomes sapāko (one who cooks dogs). Tantaṃ vāyatīti becomes tantavāyo (weaver). Varaṃ āharatīti becomes varāharo (one who brings a boon). With words ending in the suffixes -nta, -māna, and -tavant, only an uncompounded phrase is used. For example: dhammaṃ suṇanto (hearing the Dhamma), dhammaṃ suṇamāno (hearing the Dhamma), odanaṃ bhuttavā (one who has eaten rice).

Tatiyātappuriso kitaka+pubba+sadisa+samo+nattha+kalaha+nipuṇa+missa+sakhilādīhi. Buddhena bhāsito buddhabhāsito dhammo, evaṃ jinadesito. Satthārā vaṇṇito satthuvaṇṇito. Viññūhi garahito viññugarahito, viññuppasattho, issarakataṃ, sayaṃ kataṃ, sukehi āhaṭaṃ sukāhaṭaṃ, raññā hato rājahato, rājapīḷito. Agginā daḍḍho aggidaḍḍho, sappena daṭṭho sappadaṭṭho, sallehi viddho sallaviddho, icchāya pakato icchāpakato, sīlasampanno. Evaṃ sukhasahagataṃ, ñāṇasampayuttaṃ, mittasaṃsaggo, piyavippayogo, jātithaddho, guṇahīno, guṇavuddho, catuvaggakaraṇīyaṃ, catuvaggādikattabbaṃ. Kākehi peyyā kākapeyyā, nadī. Kvaci vuttiyeva, urasā gacchatīti urago, pādena pivatīti pādapo. Kvaci vākyameva, pharasunā chinnavā, kākehi pātabbā, dassanena pahātabbā. Pubbādiyoge-māsena pubbo māsapubbo. Evaṃ mātusadiso, mātusamo. Ekūnavīsati, sīlavikalo, asikalaho, vācānipuṇo, yāvakālikasammissaṃ, vācāsakhilo[M 0.0140]. Satthārā sadiso satthusadiso, satthukappo, puññena atthiko puññatthiko, guṇādhiko. Dadhinā upasittaṃ bhojanaṃ dadhibhojanaṃ, guḷena saṃsaṭṭho odano guḷodano. Kārakasambandho kriyāya kato, upasittādikriyānaṃ apaññāyanepi vuttiyevo+pasittādikriyāna+mākhyāpanato natthā+yuttatthatā. Evaṃ khīrodano. Assena yutto ratho assaratho, maggacittaṃ, jambuyā paññāto lakkhito dīpo jambudīpo, ekena adhikā dasa ekādasa, jātiyā andho jaccandho, pakatiyā medhāvī pakatimedhāvī iccādi.

The third Tappurisa compound is formed with words such as kitaka (made), pubba (former), sadisa (similar), sama (equal), nattha (destroyed), kalaha (quarrel), nipuṇa (skilled), missa (mixed), sakhila (friendly), and so on. The Dhamma spoken by the Buddha is buddhabhāsito; similarly, jinadesito. Praised by the Teacher is satthuvaṇṇito. Censured by the wise is viññugarahito; praised by the wise, viññuppasattho; made by the Lord, issarakataṃ; self-made, sayaṃ kataṃ; brought by parrots, sukāhaṭaṃ; struck by the king, rājahato; oppressed by the king, rājapīḷito. Burned by fire is aggidaḍḍho; bitten by a snake, sappadaṭṭho; pierced by arrows, sallaviddho; produced by desire, icchāpakato; endowed with virtue, sīlasampanno. Similarly: sukhasahagataṃ (accompanied by happiness), ñāṇasampayuttaṃ (associated with knowledge), mittasaṃsaggo (association with friends), piyavippayogo (separation from the beloved), jātithaddho (stubborn by birth), guṇahīno (devoid of virtues), guṇavuddho (advanced in virtues), catuvaggakaraṇīyaṃ (to be done by a group of four), catuvaggādikattabbaṃ (to be done by a group of four, etc.). Drinkable by crows is kākapeyyā, a river. Sometimes it is simply a compound expression: one that goes on its chest (urasā gacchati) is an urago (serpent); one that drinks with its foot (pādena pivati) is a pādapo (tree). Sometimes it is just a phrase: cut with an axe; to be drunk by crows; to be abandoned through seeing. In connection with pubba and so on: earlier by a month (māsena pubbo) is māsapubbo. Similarly, mātusadiso (similar to the mother), mātusamo (equal to the mother). Ekūnavīsati (one less than twenty), sīlavikalo (deficient in virtue), asikalaho (a quarrel with a sword), vācānipuṇo (skilled in speech), yāvakālikasammissaṃ (mixed for a time), vācāsakhilo (gentle in speech). Similar to the Teacher (Satthārā sadiso) is satthusadiso or satthukappo. Desiring merit (puññena atthiko) is puññatthiko; superior in virtues, guṇādhiko. Food sprinkled with curd is dadhibhojanaṃ; rice mixed with molasses is guḷodano. The case relationship is formed by the action; even when actions such as upasitta are not apparent, there is no incongruity of meaning, because the compound expression itself implies such actions. Similarly, khīrodano (milk-rice). A chariot yoked with a horse is assaratho; maggacittaṃ (path-consciousness); the island known and marked by the Jambu tree is Jambudīpo; ten increased by one is ekādasa (eleven); blind by birth is jaccandho; wise by nature is pakatimedhāvī, and so on.

Catutthītappuriso tadattha+attha+hita+deyyādīhi. Tadatthe-kathinassa dussaṃ kathinadussaṃ, kathinacīvarassāti attho. Evaṃ cīvaradussaṃ, cīvaramūlaṃ, yāguyā atthāya taṇḍulā yāgutaṇḍulā, bhattataṇḍulā, saṅghassa atthāya bhattaṃ saṅghabhattaṃ, āgantukabhattaṃ, evaṃ gamikabhattaṃ, pāsādāya dabbaṃ pāsādadabbaṃ. Ettha cā+yaṃ niccasamāso, tassa tiliṅgatā ca-bhikkhusaṅghassa attho vihāro bhikkhusaṅghattho vihāro, bhikkhusaṅghatthā yāgu, bhikkhusaṅghatthaṃ cīvaraṃ. Yassa attho yadattho, yadatthā, yadatthaṃ. Evaṃ tadattho, tadatthā, tadatthaṃ. Tathā lokahito. Buddhassa deyyaṃ buddhadeyyaṃ pupphaṃ. Saṅghadeyyaṃ cīvaraṃ. Idha na hoti “saṅghassa dātabbaṃ”.

The fourth Tappurisa compound is formed with words such as tadattha (for that purpose), attha (purpose), hita (welfare), deyya (to be given), and so on. In the sense of tadattha: kathinadussaṃ is cloth for the Kathina, meaning cloth for the Kathina robe. Similarly, cīvaradussaṃ (robe-cloth), cīvaramūlaṃ (price for a robe); rice for the purpose of gruel is yāgutaṇḍulā (gruel-rice); bhattataṇḍulā (meal-rice); food for the purpose of the Saṅgha is saṅghabhattaṃ (Saṅgha-food); āgantukabhattaṃ (guest-food); similarly, gamikabhattaṃ (traveler-food); material for the purpose of a palace is pāsādadabbaṃ (palace-material). And here, this is an invariable compound (niccasamāso), and it can be in the three genders: bhikkhusaṅghattho vihāro (a monastery for the benefit of the community of bhikkhus), bhikkhusaṅghatthā yāgu (gruel for the benefit of the community of bhikkhus), bhikkhusaṅghatthaṃ cīvaraṃ (a robe for the benefit of the community of bhikkhus). Yadattho, yadatthā, yadatthaṃ (for whose benefit). Similarly, tadattho, tadatthā, tadatthaṃ (for that purpose). Likewise, lokahito (beneficial to the world). A flower to be offered to the Buddha is buddhadeyyaṃ. A robe to be offered to the Saṅgha is saṅghadeyyaṃ. Here, the compound is not formed from the phrase 'to be given to the Saṅgha'.

Pañcamītappuriso apagamana+bhaya+virati+mocanatthādīhi. Methunasmā apeto methunāpeto, evaṃ palāpagato, nagaraniggato, piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto, kāmato nikkhantaṃ kāmanikkhantaṃ, rukkhaggā patito rukkhaggapatito, sāsanaccuto, āpatti- vuṭṭhānaṃ[M 0.0141], dharaṇītalaggato, sabbabhavehi nissaṭo sabbabhavanissaṭo. Bhayatādiyoge-rājato bhayaṃ rājabhayaṃ, corabhayaṃ, amanussabhayaṃ, aggibhayaṃ, pāpabhīto, pāpabhīruko. Akattabbato virati akattabbavirati, evaṃ kāyaduccaritavirati, vacīduccaritavirati. Bandhanā mutto bandhanamutto, vanamutto, bandhanamokkho. Kammasamuṭṭhitaṃ, ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭhaṃ, omakomakaṃ. Kvaci vuttiyeva, kammato jātaṃ kammajaṃ, evaṃ cittajaṃ, utujaṃ, āhārajaṃ. Idha na hoti ‘pāsādā patito’.

The fifth Tappurisa compound is formed with words having the sense of departure (apagamana), fear (bhaya), abstinence (virati), liberation (mocana), and so on. One who has departed from sexual intercourse (methunasmā apeto) is methunāpeto. Similarly, palāpagato (gone away), nagaraniggato (gone out of the city), piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto (returned from alms-gathering); that which has gone forth from sensual pleasures (kāmato nikkhantaṃ) is kāmanikkhantaṃ; one who has fallen from a treetop (rukkhaggā patito) is rukkhaggapatito; sāsanaccuto (fallen from the Dispensation); āpattivutthānaṃ (emergence from an offense); dharaṇītalaggato (gone from the surface of the earth); one who has gone forth from all states of existence (sabbabhavehi nissaṭo) is sabbabhavanissaṭo. In connection with fear and so on: fear from a king (rājato bhayaṃ) is rājabhayaṃ; corabhayaṃ (fear of thieves), amanussabhayaṃ (fear of non-human beings), aggibhayaṃ (fear of fire); pāpabhīto (afraid of evil), pāpabhīruko (timid of evil). Abstinence from what should not be done (akattabbato virati) is akattabbavirati. Similarly, kāyaduccaritavirati (abstinence from bodily misconduct), vacīduccaritavirati (abstinence from verbal misconduct). One who is freed from bondage (bandhanā mutto) is bandhanamutto; vanamutto (freed from the forest); bandhanamokkho (liberation from bondage). Kammasamuṭṭhitaṃ (arisen from kamma), ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭhaṃ (highest of the high), omakomakaṃ (lowest of the low). Sometimes it is simply a compound expression: born from kamma (kammato jātaṃ) is kammajaṃ. Similarly, cittajaṃ (born of mind), utujaṃ (born of season), āhārajaṃ (born of nutriment). Here, the compound is not formed from the phrase 'fallen from a palace'.

Chaṭṭhītappuriso rañño putto rājaputto, evaṃ rājapuriso, ācariyapūjako, buddhasāvako, buddharūpaṃ, jinavacanaṃ, samuddaghoso, dhaññānaṃ rāsi dhaññarāsi, pupphagandho, phalaraso, kāyassa lahutā kāyalahutā. Maraṇassati, rukkhamūlaṃ, ayassa patto ayopatto, ettha “manādyāpādīna+mo maye ce”ti o. Evaṃ suvaṇṇakaṭāhaṃ, pānīyathālakaṃ, sappikumbho, devānaṃ rājā devarājā. Pumassa liṅgaṃ pulliṅgaṃ, “puṃ pumassavā”ti pumassa puṃ, niggahītalopo, lassa dvibhāvo ca. Hatthipadaṃ, itthirūpaṃ, bhikkhunisaṅgho, jambusākhā, ettha īkārūkārānaṃ rasso. Bahulādhikārā nta+māna+niddhāriya+pūraṇa+bhāva+tittatthehi na hoti. Mamā+nukubbaṃ, mamā+nukurumāno, gunnaṃ kaṇhā sampannakhīratamā, sissānaṃ pañcamo, paṭassa suttatā. Kvaci hoteva ‘vattamānasāmīpyaṃ’. Brāhmaṇassa sukkā dantāti sāpekkhatāya na hoti. Phalānaṃ titto, phalāna+māsito, phalānaṃ suhito. “Brāhmaṇassa uccaṃ gehaṃ”ti sāpekkhatāya na hoti. “Rañño pāṭaliputtakassa dhanaṃ”ti dhanasambandhe [M 0.0142] chaṭṭhīti pāṭaliputtakena sambandhābhāvā na hoti. “Rañño go ca asso ca puriso cā”ti bhinnatthatāya vākyameva. Rañño gavassapurisā rājagavassapurisāti vutti hoteva, ekatthībhāvā. Sambandhīsaddānaṃ pana niccasāpekkhattepi gamakattā samāso, gamakattampi hi samāsassa nibandhanaṃ, yathā devadattassa gurukulaṃ, bhagavato sāvakasaṅghotiādi.

The sixth Tappurisa compound: the king's son (rañño putto) is rājaputto. Similarly, rājapuriso (king's man), ācariyapūjako (worshipper of a teacher), buddhasāvako (disciple of the Buddha), buddharūpaṃ (form of the Buddha), jinavacanaṃ (word of the Victor), samuddaghoso (roar of the ocean). A heap of grains (dhaññānaṃ rāsi) is dhaññarāsi. Pupphagandho (fragrance of a flower), phalaraso (juice of a fruit). Lightness of the body (kāyassa lahutā) is kāyalahutā. Maraṇassati (mindfulness of death), rukkhamūlaṃ (root of a tree). A bowl of iron (ayassa patto) is ayopatto; here, the 'o' is formed by the rule 'manādyāpādīnamo maye ce'. Similarly, suvaṇṇakaṭāhaṃ (golden pan), pānīyathālakaṃ (drinking bowl), sappikumbho (pot of ghee). The king of the gods (devānaṃ rājā) is devarājā. The gender of a male (pumassa liṅgaṃ) is pulliṅgaṃ; by the rule 'puṃ pumassavā', 'pumassa' becomes 'puṃ', with the elision of the niggahīta and the doubling of 'l'. Hatthipadaṃ (foot of an elephant), itthirūpaṃ (form of a woman), bhikkhunisaṅgho (community of bhikkhunīs), jambusākhā (branch of a Jambu tree); here, the long vowels 'ī' and 'ū' are shortened. Due to the governing rule of general applicability, compounding does not occur with words ending in -nta and -māna, or in the sense of specification (niddhāriya), ordinal numbers (pūraṇa), state (bhāva), and satisfaction (titta). For example: mamānukubbaṃ (imitating me), mamānukurumāno (imitating me); gunnaṃ kaṇhā sampannakhīratamā (the black one among the cows, the most abundant in milk); sissānaṃ pañcamo (the fifth of the disciples); paṭassa suttatā (the state of being thread of the cloth). Sometimes it does occur, for example, vattamānasāmīpyaṃ (proximity to the present). The phrase 'brāhmaṇassa sukkā dantā' (the brahmin's white teeth) does not form a compound due to its dependence on an external word. The phrases 'phalānaṃ titto' (satisfied with fruits), 'phalānamāsito' (satiated with fruits), 'phalānaṃ suhito' (content with fruits) do not form compounds. The phrase 'brāhmaṇassa uccaṃ gehaṃ' (the brahmin's high house) does not form a compound due to its dependence on an external word. In the phrase 'rañño pāṭaliputtakassa dhanaṃ' (the wealth of the king of Pāṭaliputta), the genitive is in relation to 'wealth', so there is no compounding because there is no connection with 'Pāṭaliputtaka'. The phrase 'rañño go ca asso ca puriso ca' (the king's cow and horse and man) is merely a sentence due to the distinct meanings. However, 'rañño gavassapurisā' can be compounded as 'rājagavassapurisā' because it conveys a single meaning. For relational words, however, even when constantly dependent, compounding occurs because it is intelligible, for intelligibility is indeed a basis for compounding, as in 'devadattassa gurukulaṃ' (Devadatta's teacher's family), 'bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho' (the Blessed One's community of disciples), and so on.

Sattamītappuriso rūpe saññā rūpasaññā, evaṃ rūpasañcetanā, saṃsāradukkhaṃ. Cakkhumhi sannissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Dhamme rato dhammarato, dhammābhirati, dhammaruci, dhammagāravo, dhammesu nirutti dhammanirutti, dānādhimutti, bhavantarakataṃ. Dassane assādo dassanassādo. Araññe vāso araññavāso, vikālabhojanaṃ, kālavassaṃ, vanapupphaṃ, vanamahiso, gāmasūkaro, samuddamacchā, āvāṭakacchapo, āvāṭamaṇḍūko, kūpamaṇḍūko, titthanāvā. Itthīsu dhutto itthidhutto, akkhadhutto. Chāyāyaṃ sukkho chāyāsukkho, aṅgārapakkaṃ, cārakavano. Kvaci vuttiyeva, vane caratīti vanacarako, kucchimhi sayantīti kucchisayā, thale tiṭṭhatīti thalaṭṭho, jalaṭṭho, pabbataṭṭho, maggaṭṭho. Paṅke jātaṃ paṅkajaṃ, saroruha+miccādi. Idha na hoti, bhojane mattaññutā, indriyesu guttadvāratā, āsane nisinno, āsane nisīditabbaṃ.

The seventh Tappurisa compound: perception in form (rūpe saññā) is rūpasaññā. Similarly, rūpasañcetanā (volition regarding form), saṃsāradukkhaṃ (suffering in saṃsāra). Consciousness based in the eye (cakkhumhi sannissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ) is cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. One who delights in the Dhamma (dhamme rato) is dhammarato; dhammābhirati (delight in the Dhamma), dhammaruci (inclination for the Dhamma), dhammagāravo (reverence for the Dhamma). Expertise in the Dhamma (dhammesu nirutti) is dhammanirutti; dānādhimutti (resolve on giving), bhavantarakataṃ (done in another existence). Pleasure in seeing (dassane assādo) is dassanassādo. Dwelling in the forest (araññe vāso) is araññavāso; vikālabhojanaṃ (eating at the wrong time), kālavassaṃ (rain in season), vanapupphaṃ (forest flower), vanamahiso (wild buffalo), gāmasūkaro (village pig), samuddamacchā (sea fish), āvāṭakacchapo (pit tortoise), āvāṭamaṇḍūko (pit frog), kūpamaṇḍūko (well frog), titthanāvā (ferry boat). A rogue in regard to women (itthīsu dhutto) is itthidhutto; akkhadhutto (a rogue in regard to dice). Dried in the shade (chāyāyaṃ sukkho) is chāyāsukkho; aṅgārapakkaṃ (cooked on embers), cārakavano (a wanderer's forest). Sometimes it is simply a compound expression: one who wanders in the forest (vane carati) is vanacarako; those that lie in the womb (kucchimhi sayanti) are kucchisayā; one that stands on land (thale tiṭṭhati) is thalaṭṭho; jalaṭṭho (standing in water), pabbataṭṭho (standing on a mountain), maggaṭṭho (standing on a road). Born in the mud (paṅke jātaṃ) is paṅkajaṃ; saroruha (grown in a lake), and so on. Here, compounding does not occur in phrases such as: bhojane mattaññutā (moderation in food), indriyesu guttadvāratā (guarding the doors of the senses), āsane nisinno (seated on a seat), āsane nisīditabbaṃ (one should sit on a seat).

11. Visesana+mekatthena

11. A qualifier having a single meaning.

Visesanaṃ syādyantaṃ visessena syādyantena samānādhikaraṇenasahe+katthaṃ hoti.

An inflected qualifier becomes one in meaning with an inflected qualified word that is in apposition.

Samānatthe [M 0.0143] pade yattha, bhedyabhedakavācake;

Visesanasamāso+yaṃ, visessatthapadhānato.

Where words are of the same meaning, expressing the distinguished and the distinguisher, this is a qualifier compound, because the meaning of the qualified is primary.

Visessagata+meva+tra, liṅga+metaṃ paraṃ tato;

Kammadhāraya+micce+sa, samāso+ññehi saññito.

Here, indeed, this gender and so forth pertains to the qualified and is subsequent thereto. This compound is designated Kammadhāraya by others.

Sutte visessenāti avuttepi visesanassa sambandhīsaddattā sāmatthiyato labbhamānaākaḍḍhitasaddaṃ pati “visessenā”ti vuttaṃ. Vuttañca –

Although 'visessena' is not stated in the sutta, 'visessena' is said with reference to the word that is obtained and supplied by virtue of its capacity, because it is a word related to the qualifier. And it is said:

Sāmaññavatthu yā vattha+ntarato tu visesiya;

Ekappakāre ṭhapanā, visesana+mitī+ritaṃ.

The establishing in one mode of a general thing, which is to be distinguished from another thing, is called a qualifier.

Ekappakāragaṃ vatthu, visessanti pavuccati;

Padāni yāni yāneva, sambandha+mupayanti+ha;

Gamyate kāmacārena, visesana+visessatāti.

A thing that has gone into one mode is called the qualified. Whatever words, indeed, attain a connection here, the state of being a qualifier and qualified is understood by convention.

Ettha ca uppaladabbaṃ rattuppalādito visesayatīti nīlasaddo visesanaṃ. Tena visesiyatīti uppalasaddo visessaṃ. Api ca bhamara+ṅgārādisāmañña nīlatthato visesiyatīti nīlaṃ visessaṃ. Na vatthādīnaṃ, uppalassevāti visesanato uppalaṃ visesanaṃti kāmacāreneti vuttaṃ. Api ca –

Here, the word 'blue' is the qualifier because it distinguishes the lotus-substance from red lotuses and so forth. The word 'lotus' is the qualified because it is qualified by that. Moreover, 'blue' is the qualified because it is distinguished from the general meaning of blue found in bees, charcoal, and so forth. Not of cloths and so forth, but of the lotus itself—because it thus qualifies, 'lotus' is the qualifier. Hence it is said 'by convention'. Moreover:

Parito ayantya+nena+tthā, pariyāyoti vuccati;

Govācāti pavutte tu, vācattho tu visesanaṃ.

That by which meanings are approached from all sides is called a pariyāya. But when 'govāca' is stated, the meaning of 'vāca' is the qualifier.

Visesse dissamānā yā, liṅga+saṃkhyā+vibhattiyo;

Tulyādhikaraṇe bhiyyo, kattabbā tā visesaneti –

Whatever genders, numbers, and case-endings are seen in the qualified, those should, for the most part, be made the same in the qualifier when in apposition.

Vuttattā mahanto+ccādīsu samānaliṅgādayo daṭṭhabbā. Bhiyyoti kiṃ, devā pamāṇaṃ iccādi.

Because it has been said, in 'mahanto' and so forth, the same gender and so on are to be seen. Why 'for the most part'? For example, 'devā pamāṇaṃ' (the gods are the standard), and so forth.

So [M 0.0144] ca chabbidho visesanapubbapado, visesanuttarapado, visesanobhayapado, upamānuttarapado, sambhāvanāpubbapado, avadhāraṇapubbapadoti.

And it is of six kinds: that with the qualifier as the first member, that with the qualifier as the final member, that with qualifiers as both members, that with a simile as the final member, that with conception as the first member, and that with emphasis as the first member.

Tattha visesanapubbapade tāva-mahanto ca so puriso cāti vākye iminā suttena samāso. “Ṭa nta+ntūnaṃ”ti ntassa ṭādese dīgho hoti, mahāpuriso, mahāpurisā iccādi.

Herein, firstly, in the case of the qualifier-preceding-member: in the phrase 'mahanto ca so puriso ca', the compound is formed by this rule. By the rule 'Ṭa nta-ntūnaṃ', when `ā` is substituted for `nta`, the vowel is lengthened, thus `mahāpuriso`, `mahāpurisā`, and so forth.

Vākye tulyādhikaraṇabhāva pakāsanatthaṃ ca+ta-saddapayogo. Vuttiyantu samāseneva tappakāsanato na tappayogo. Eva+maññatrāpi vuttatthāna+mappayogo. Evaṃ mahāvīro, mahāmuni. Mahantañca taṃ balañcāti mahābalaṃ, mahabbhayaṃ. Santo ca so puriso cāti sappuriso. Tathā pubbapuriso, aparapuriso, paṭhamapuriso, majjhimapuriso, uttamapuriso, parapuriso, setahatthī, kaṇhasappo, nīluppalaṃ, rattuppalaṃ, lohitacandanaṃ. Kvaci na hoti, puṇṇo mantānīputto, citto gahapati. Pumā ca so kokilo cāti puṅkokilo, uttarapade pumassa puṃ hoti. Evaṃ punnāgo.

In a sentence, the use of the words `ca` and `ta` is for the purpose of indicating the state of being in apposition. But in a compound, since that is indicated by the compound itself, they are not used. Likewise, elsewhere too, what has been expressed by the components is not employed. Thus, `mahāvīro` (great hero), `mahāmuni` (great sage). `Mahantañca taṃ balañca` becomes `mahābalaṃ` (great strength), `mahabbhayaṃ` (great fear). `Santo ca so puriso ca` becomes `sappuriso` (good man). Similarly, `pubbapuriso` (former man), `aparapuriso` (later man), `paṭhamapuriso` (first man), `majjhimapuriso` (middle man), `uttamapuriso` (highest man), `parapuriso` (other man), `setahatthī` (white elephant), `kaṇhasappo` (black serpent), `nīluppalaṃ` (blue lotus), `rattuppalaṃ` (red lotus), `lohitacandanaṃ` (red sandalwood). In some cases, compounding does not occur, as in `puṇṇo mantānīputto` (Puṇṇa, son of Mantānī), `citto gahapati` (Citta the householder). `Pumā ca so kokilo ca` becomes `puṅkokilo` (male cuckoo); when a word follows, `puma` becomes `puṃ`. Similarly, `punnāgo` (male nāga tree).

Khattiyā ca sā kaññā cāti khattiyakaññā.

`Khattiyā ca sā kaññā ca` (a noblewoman and that maiden) becomes `khattiyakaññā` (noble maiden).

67. Itthiyaṃ bhāsitapumi+tthī pumeve+kattheti

67. A feminine word that has a corresponding masculine form becomes like the masculine when conveying a single meaning.

Bhāsitapumā itthī pumeva hotīti pumbhāvā itthipaccayānaṃ nivatti hoti. Evaṃ rattalatā, dutiyabhikkhā. Brāhmaṇī ca sā dārikā cāti brāhmaṇadārikā, nāgamāṇavikā. Itthiyanti kiṃ, kumāriratanaṃ, samaṇipadumaṃ. Bhāsitapumāti kiṃ, gaṅgānadī, taṇhānadī[M 0.0145], pathavīdhātu. Puratthimo ca so kāyo cāti puratthimakāyo. Ettha ca kāyekadese kāyasaddo. Evaṃ pacchimakāyo, uparimakāyo, heṭṭhimakāyo, sabbakāyo, navāvāso, kataranikāyo, hetupaccayo. Jīvitappadhānaṃ navakaṃ jīvitanavaka+miccādi.

A feminine word with a corresponding masculine form becomes like the masculine; thus, due to this masculine state, there is a removal of the feminine suffixes. For example, `rattalatā` (red creeper), `dutiyabhikkhā` (second alms). `Brāhmaṇī ca sā dārikā ca` (a Brahmin woman and that girl) becomes `brāhmaṇadārikā` (Brahmin girl); `nāgamāṇavikā` (nāga maiden). Why the condition 'feminine'? For example: `kumāriratanaṃ` (maiden-jewel), `samaṇipadumaṃ` (ascetic-lotus). Why the condition 'with a corresponding masculine form'? For example: `gaṅgānadī` (river Ganges), `taṇhānadī` (river of craving), `pathavīdhātu` (earth element). `Puratthimo ca so kāyo ca` (eastern and that body) becomes `puratthimakāyo` (eastern part of the body). Here the word `kāya` denotes a part of the body. Similarly, `pacchimakāyo` (western part of the body), `uparimakāyo` (upper part of the body), `heṭṭhimakāyo` (lower part of the body), `sabbakāyo` (entire body), `navāvāso` (new residence), `kataranikāyo` (which group), `hetupaccayo` (root condition). `Jīvitappadhānaṃ navakaṃ` (the nonad of which life is primary) becomes `jīvitanavakaṃ`, and so forth.

Visesanuttarapade therā+cariya+paṇḍitā visesanaṃ parañca bhavati. Yathā sāriputto ca so thero cāti sāriputtatthero, evaṃ mahāmoggallānatthero, mahākassapatthero, buddhaghosācariyo, dhammapālācariyo, ācariyaguttilo vā. Mahosadho ca so paṇḍito cāti mahosadhapaṇḍito, evaṃ vidhurapaṇḍito.

In the qualifier-following-member compound, the words `thera` (elder), `ācariya` (teacher), and `paṇḍita` (wise one) are qualifiers and are placed second. For example, `sāriputto ca so thero ca` (Sāriputta and that elder) becomes `sāriputtatthero` (the elder Sāriputta); similarly, `mahāmoggallānatthero` (the elder Mahāmoggallāna), `mahākassapatthero` (the elder Mahākassapa), `buddhaghosācariyo` (the teacher Buddhaghosa), `dhammapālācariyo` (the teacher Dhammapāla), or `ācariyaguttilo` (the teacher Guttila). `Mahosadho ca so paṇḍito ca` (Mahosadha and that wise one) becomes `mahosadhapaṇḍito` (the wise Mahosadha); similarly, `vidhurapaṇḍito` (the wise Vidhura).

Visesanobhayapade yathā-sītañca taṃ uṇhañcāti sītuṇhaṃ, siniddho ca so uṇho cāti siniddhuṇho māso. Khañjo ca so khujjo cāti khañjakhujjo, evaṃ andhabadhiro, katākataṃ, chiddāvachiddaṃ, uccāvacaṃ, chinnabhinnaṃ, gatapaccāgataṃ. Kvaci pubbakālassāpi paranipāto, vāsito ca so litto cāti littavāsito, evaṃ naggamūsito, sittasammaṭṭho, bhaṭṭhaluñjito.

In the qualifier-both-members compound, for example: `sītañca taṃ uṇhañca` (cold and that hot) becomes `sītuṇhaṃ` (cold and hot); `siniddho ca so uṇho ca` (smooth and that hot) becomes `siniddhuṇho māso` (a smooth and hot month). `Khañjo ca so khujjo ca` (lame and that hunchbacked) becomes `khañjakhujjo` (lame and hunchbacked); similarly, `andhabadhiro` (blind and deaf), `katākataṃ` (done and undone), `chiddāvachiddaṃ` (with and without holes), `uccāvacaṃ` (high and low), `chinnabhinnaṃ` (cut and broken), `gatapaccāgataṃ` (gone and returned). Sometimes, even what is prior in time is placed second: `vāsito ca so litto ca` (perfumed and that smeared) becomes `littavāsito` (smeared and perfumed); similarly, `naggamūsito` (stripped and robbed), `sittasammaṭṭho` (sprinkled and swept), `bhaṭṭhaluñjito` (roasted and plucked).

Upamanuttarapade upamānabhūtaṃ visesanaṃ paraṃ bhavati, yathā sīhoti vutte upacaritā+nupacaritasīhānaṃ sāmaññappatītiyaṃ munisaddo viseseti. Ettha ca –

In the simile-following-member compound, the qualifier, which is the simile, is placed second. For example, when 'lion' is said, giving rise to a general understanding of both metaphorical and literal lions, the word 'sage' specifies. And in this connection:

Upamāno+pameyyānaṃ, sadhammattaṃ siyo+pamā.

A simile consists in the state of having a common property between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison.

Sā ca vatthu+vaṇṇa+ākārānaṃ sāmyena hoti. Sīhova sīho, muni ca so sīho cāti munisīho, munivasabho, munipuṅgavo[M 0.0146], buddhanāgo, buddhādicco. Raṃsī viya raṃsī, saddhammo ca so raṃsī cāti saddhammaraṃsī, evaṃ vinayasāgaro. Puṇḍarikamiva puṇḍariko, samaṇo ca so puṇḍariko cāti samaṇapuṇḍariko, samaṇapadumo. Cando viya cando, mukhañca taṃ cando cāti mukhacando, mukhapadumaṃ iccādi.

And that occurs through similarity of substance, color, and form. As a lion is a lion, so `muni ca so sīho ca` (the sage and he is a lion) becomes `munisīho` (sage-lion); `munivasabho` (sage-bull), `munipuṅgavo` (sage-chief), `buddhanāgo` (Buddha-nāga), `buddhādicco` (Buddha-sun). As a ray is a ray, so `saddhammo ca so raṃsī ca` (the good Dhamma and it is a ray) becomes `saddhammaraṃsī` (ray of the good Dhamma); similarly `vinayasāgaro` (ocean of discipline). As a white lotus is a white lotus, so `samaṇo ca so puṇḍariko ca` (the ascetic and he is a white lotus) becomes `samaṇapuṇḍariko` (ascetic-white-lotus), `samaṇapadumo` (ascetic-lotus). As the moon is the moon, so `mukhañca taṃ cando ca` (the face and it is the moon) becomes `mukhacando` (face-moon), `mukhapadumaṃ` (face-lotus), and so forth.

Sambhāvanāpubbapade yathā-dhammoti buddhi dhammabuddhi, evaṃ dhammasaññā, dhammasaṅkhāto, dhammasammato, pāṇasaññitā, asubhasaññā, aniccasaññā, dhātusaññā, attasaññā, attadiṭṭhi iccādi.
